questions.q: Which term BEST describes land, all permanent natural objects, and all permanent man-made improvements attached to it?

opts.A: Personal property
opts.B: Appurtenance
opts.C: Chattel
opts.D: Real estate

questions.exp: Real estate = land + everything permanently attached (natural or artificial). "Land" alone excludes improvements; "real property" adds the bundle of legal rights.

questions.q: The "bundle of legal rights" is included in the definition of:

opts.A: Real property
opts.B: Personal property
opts.C: Real estate
opts.D: Appurtenance

questions.exp: Real property = real estate + the bundle of legal rights (possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, disposition). Real estate alone does not include these rights.

questions.q: A homeowner cuts down a tree in her backyard for firewood. Which legal concept describes what happened to the tree?

opts.A: Annexation
opts.B: Severance
opts.C: Accession
opts.D: Emblements

questions.exp: Severance converts real property into personal property — the tree (real estate while standing) became a chattel once cut. Annexation is the opposite: personal property becoming real property.

questions.q: A tenant operates a diner and installs a commercial deep fryer that is bolted to the floor. When the lease ends, the tenant may:

opts.A: Never remove it because it is a fixture
opts.B: Remove it only if the landlord provides a replacement
opts.C: Remove it only with written court approval
opts.D: Remove it as a trade fixture before vacating

questions.exp: Trade fixtures — equipment used in a business, attached by a tenant — remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed on or before the last day of tenancy. Damage must be repaired.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three legal tests used to determine whether an item is a fixture?

opts.A: Method of annexation
opts.B: Adaptation to real estate
opts.C: Purchase price of the item
opts.D: Agreement of the parties

questions.exp: Courts use method of annexation, adaptation, and agreement to decide fixture status. Purchase price has no bearing on the determination.

questions.q: Corn growing in a field that was planted and cultivated by a tenant farmer is considered:

opts.A: Real property because it is attached to the land
opts.B: Personal property (emblements) belonging to the tenant
opts.C: A fixture belonging to the landlord
opts.D: Real property until harvested by the landlord

questions.exp: Annual crops requiring cultivation are called emblements (fructus industriales) and are personal property. The tenant who planted them is entitled to harvest them even after the tenancy ends.

questions.q: A buyer purchases a house. The seller removes a built-in bookcase that was custom-fitted to an alcove. The buyer's BEST legal argument is that:

opts.A: The bookcase was personal property and the seller may take it
opts.B: The seller needs only to disclose removal in the listing
opts.C: The bookcase was adapted to the property and is a fixture
opts.D: Built-in items are always excluded from the sale

questions.exp: Custom adaptation to an alcove suggests the item was intended as a permanent part of the property — a key test of a fixture. The buyer has a strong argument for its inclusion in the sale.

questions.q: An owner sells the surface rights to her farm but retains the subsurface rights. A mining company later discovers oil beneath the property. Who owns the oil?

opts.A: The original owner who retained subsurface rights
opts.B: The state of Pennsylvania
opts.C: The new surface owner
opts.D: The federal government

questions.exp: Subsurface (mineral) rights can be severed from surface rights and transferred separately. The original owner retained the oil by keeping the subsurface rights.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, a manufactured home is treated as real estate when:

opts.A: It is wider than 12 feet
opts.B: It has been occupied for more than two years
opts.C: It is permanently attached to a foundation AND its motor vehicle registration is canceled
opts.D: It is placed on a concrete slab

questions.exp: PA requires two conditions: (1) permanent attachment to a foundation, and (2) cancellation of the motor vehicle registration with the PA Bureau of Motor Vehicles. Both must occur.

questions.q: The primary purpose of real estate license laws in Pennsylvania is to:

opts.A: Protect the public from fraud, dishonesty, and incompetence
opts.B: Create employment opportunities in the real estate industry
opts.C: Generate revenue for the state through licensing fees
opts.D: Set standard commission rates for all brokers

questions.exp: All state license laws share the same core purpose: protecting the public. They are not designed to set fees, control commissions, or create jobs.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, the seller of a property located in a coal mining area is required to provide the buyer with a:

opts.A: Radon disclosure form
opts.B: Lead paint disclosure
opts.C: Flood zone certificate
opts.D: Coal Mining Notice

questions.exp: Pennsylvania law requires a Coal Mining Notice disclosing whether the structure is protected from subsidence caused by underground coal mining. Special insurance (mine subsidence insurance) may be available.

questions.q: Which of the following rights allows a property owner to keep others from entering or using their property?

opts.A: Right of enjoyment
opts.B: Right of exclusion
opts.C: Right of disposition
opts.D: Right of possession

questions.exp: The right of exclusion is the right to keep others off the property. Right of enjoyment = using it lawfully; right of possession = occupying it; right of disposition = selling or transferring it.

questions.q: A right or privilege that runs with the land and transfers automatically when the property is sold is called a(n):

opts.A: Appurtenance
opts.B: Fixture
opts.C: Chattel
opts.D: Encumbrance

questions.exp: An appurtenance — such as a parking space, easement, or water right — is attached to the property and transfers with it to each new owner unless specifically excluded.

questions.q: Which characteristic of land refers to the fact that each parcel is unique and no two parcels are exactly alike?

opts.A: Nonhomogeneity
opts.B: Indestructibility
opts.C: Immobility
opts.D: Scarcity

questions.exp: Nonhomogeneity (uniqueness) is a physical characteristic of land — even two adjacent lots differ in soil, drainage, and position. This uniqueness is why real estate markets are highly localized.

questions.q: Personal property is conveyed (transferred) by:

opts.A: A deed
opts.B: A mortgage
opts.C: A bill of sale
opts.D: A title insurance policy

questions.exp: Deeds transfer real property. Personal property (chattels) is transferred by a bill of sale or receipt. This distinction is foundational to understanding real estate transactions.

questions.q: A real estate licensee's clients ask whether they should take title as joint tenants or tenants in common. The licensee should:

opts.A: Recommend joint tenancy because it provides survivorship rights
opts.B: Suggest they consult an attorney
opts.C: Recommend tenancy in common to maximize flexibility
opts.D: Explain both options and let them decide without legal guidance

questions.exp: Only attorneys can advise on legal matters such as how to take title. A licensee who gives legal advice is practicing law without a license, which is prohibited.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST represents a physical characteristic of land?

opts.A: Scarcity
opts.B: Area preference (situs)
opts.C: Permanence of investment
opts.D: Immobility

questions.exp: Physical characteristics include immobility, indestructibility, and nonhomogeneity. Scarcity, improvements, permanence of investment, and area preference are economic characteristics.

questions.q: Concrete poured into a foundation form was previously bagged cement mix (personal property). After pouring and curing, the concrete is:

opts.A: Still personal property because it was purchased separately
opts.B: A trade fixture removable by the contractor
opts.C: Real property through annexation
opts.D: Personal property until the building receives a certificate of occupancy

questions.exp: Annexation is the process by which personal property becomes real property when permanently incorporated into land or a structure — exactly what happens when cement becomes a foundation.

questions.q: How often must Pennsylvania real estate licensees renew their licenses?

opts.A: Every year
opts.B: Every two years
opts.C: Every three years
opts.D: Every five years

questions.exp: PA licenses renew on a two-year cycle. Renewal requires completing 14 hours of continuing education and paying the renewal fee.

questions.q: A homeowner owns a house and the land beneath it. A railroad purchased a right-of-way through the property 30 years ago. The homeowner recently built a garage that sits over the railroad easement. Which statement is TRUE?

opts.A: The railroad lost its right because it has not used the easement in many years
opts.B: The garage becomes part of the railroad's property
opts.C: The homeowner may demand compensation to remove the garage
opts.D: The railroad retains its right to use the easement area

questions.exp: An appurtenant easement or right-of-way runs with the land and is not extinguished by nonuse or by a structure built over it. The railroad retains its legal right to use — and potentially require removal of — any obstruction.

questions.q: A municipality's authority to regulate land use for the health, safety, and welfare of the public is derived from its:

opts.A: Eminent domain power
opts.B: Escheat power
opts.C: Police power
opts.D: Taxation power

questions.exp: Police power allows government to regulate private property use (zoning, building codes) without compensation. Eminent domain = taking with compensation; escheat = property reverting to state; taxation = imposing taxes.

questions.q: A gas station that legally existed before a zoning change reclassified its area as residential may continue to operate as a:

opts.A: Nonconforming use
opts.B: Special use permit
opts.C: Variance
opts.D: Conditional use

questions.exp: A nonconforming use is a use that legally existed before a zoning change but no longer complies with current zoning. It is generally allowed to continue but cannot be expanded or rebuilt if destroyed beyond a set percentage.

questions.q: A property owner requests permission to build a fence six inches higher than the zoning ordinance allows. This is an application for a:

opts.A: Special use permit
opts.B: Variance
opts.C: Rezoning
opts.D: Conditional use permit

questions.exp: A variance is an authorized deviation from specific zoning requirements for a particular parcel, granted when strict compliance would create undue hardship. It does not change the underlying zoning.

questions.q: The government takes a privately owned parcel to build a new elementary school. The owner receives fair market value. This is an exercise of:

opts.A: Police power
opts.B: Escheat
opts.C: Adverse possession
opts.D: Eminent domain

questions.exp: Eminent domain (condemnation) is the government's power to take private property for public use with just (fair market value) compensation. Police power regulates use without compensation.

questions.q: A new road widens onto a homeowner's front yard without a formal taking, substantially reducing property value. The owner's legal remedy is called:

opts.A: Inverse condemnation
opts.B: Condemnation
opts.C: Adverse possession
opts.D: Rezoning

questions.exp: Inverse condemnation is a lawsuit filed by the property owner against the government to compel payment when a government action damages or de facto takes private property without formal condemnation proceedings.

questions.q: Deed restrictions (CC&Rs) that limit a subdivision to single-family residential use are an example of:

opts.A: Government-imposed zoning
opts.B: A building code requirement
opts.C: Private land-use controls
opts.D: An encroachment

questions.exp: Deed restrictions and CC&Rs are private controls created by developers or grantor agreements. They can be more restrictive than zoning but are enforced by property owners or HOAs, not the government.

questions.q: Before a newly constructed home may be occupied, the builder must obtain a:

opts.A: Zoning variance
opts.B: Plat map
opts.C: Special use permit
opts.D: Certificate of occupancy

questions.exp: A certificate of occupancy (CO) confirms that a building complies with all applicable codes and is safe for habitation. It is issued by the local building department after a final inspection.

questions.q: A developer divides a large tract into 120 individual lots and records the legal map with the county. This recorded map is called a:

opts.A: Plat
opts.B: Benchmark
opts.C: Metes and bounds description
opts.D: Datum

questions.exp: A plat (recorded subdivision map) divides land into named lots, blocks, and streets, and is the basis for the lot-and-block method of legal description.

questions.q: Which type of zoning allows a church to operate in a residential zone because of the unique nature of its use?

opts.A: Variance
opts.B: Nonconforming use
opts.C: Special use (conditional use) permit
opts.D: Rezoning

questions.exp: A special use (or conditional use) permit allows uses that would otherwise not be permitted in a zone, provided they meet specific conditions. Churches and schools in residential areas are classic examples.

questions.q: When a person dies intestate with no heirs and no will, their real property passes to the state through the doctrine of:

opts.A: Escheat
opts.B: Police power
opts.C: Adverse possession
opts.D: Eminent domain

questions.exp: Escheat is the reversion of property to the state when the owner dies without a will and without any legal heirs. It prevents property from being ownerless.

questions.q: Cluster zoning is BEST described as:

opts.A: Zoning that requires uniform lot sizes throughout a development
opts.B: Grouping homes on smaller lots to preserve open space
opts.C: Allowing only commercial uses near highway interchanges
opts.D: Separating industrial uses from residential areas

questions.exp: Cluster zoning permits smaller individual lots than normally required, grouping homes together, in exchange for preserving common open space, parks, or natural features within the development.

questions.q: A zoning ordinance designates a strip of land between a residential area and an industrial park as a park. This strip is called a:

opts.A: Setback line
opts.B: Benchmark
opts.C: Plottage
opts.D: Buffer zone

questions.exp: A buffer zone is a transitional area (often open space, parks, or low-density uses) placed between incompatible land uses to reduce negative impacts such as noise, traffic, or visual blight.

questions.q: Two adjacent parcels are combined into one larger parcel, and the combined parcel is worth more than the sum of the two separate parcels. This INCREASE in value is called:

opts.A: Subdivision
opts.B: Plottage
opts.C: Assemblage
opts.D: Cluster development

questions.exp: Assemblage is the ACT of combining adjacent parcels; plottage is the resulting INCREASE in value, because the combined parcel is worth more than the sum of its parts. The question asks about the value increase.

questions.q: Building codes primarily regulate:

opts.A: How land may be used
opts.B: Subdivision design standards
opts.C: Environmental impact of development
opts.D: Construction standards for materials and methods

questions.exp: Building codes set minimum standards for construction quality, safety, electrical, plumbing, and structural integrity. Zoning regulates land use; subdivision regulations govern lot design.

questions.q: A developer submits plans for a new subdivision. Before the first lot can be sold, the developer typically must obtain:

opts.A: A certificate of occupancy for each lot
opts.B: Individual variance approvals for each lot
opts.C: Subdivision approval and plat recording
opts.D: Special use permits for each individual home

questions.exp: Subdivision approval (reviewing lot size, street layout, utilities) and recording of the plat with the county are prerequisites to marketing and selling lots in a new subdivision.

questions.q: A zoning ordinance requires all buildings to be set back at least 25 feet from the front property line. This requirement is called a:

opts.A: Setback (building line)
opts.B: Nonconforming setback
opts.C: Buffer zone
opts.D: Deed restriction

questions.exp: Setback requirements specify the minimum distance a structure must be from the property line, street, or other boundaries. Violations require a variance before construction.

questions.q: Private deed restrictions can be MORE restrictive than local zoning, but they:

opts.A: Override zoning if recorded earlier
opts.B: Cannot permit uses that zoning prohibits
opts.C: Are never enforceable after 10 years
opts.D: Are enforced by the local zoning board

questions.exp: Deed restrictions and zoning coexist — both must be satisfied. A restriction can add rules beyond zoning but cannot grant permission for something zoning bans. The more restrictive rule prevails.

questions.q: A comprehensive (master) plan is BEST described as:

opts.A: A legally binding zoning ordinance
opts.B: A building code for a municipality
opts.C: A long-range guide for community growth and land-use policy
opts.D: A recorded subdivision plat

questions.exp: A comprehensive plan is a policy document that guides future development — it is not legally binding on its own but forms the basis for zoning ordinances, subdivision rules, and capital improvements.

questions.q: A city requires that no building in the downtown district exceed 10 stories. This is an example of a:

opts.A: Setback requirement
opts.B: Buffer zone
opts.C: Cluster zoning rule
opts.D: Height restriction

questions.exp: Zoning ordinances can regulate building height (bulk regulations) in addition to use, lot coverage, and setbacks. Height limits protect sight lines, sunlight, and neighborhood character.

questions.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of a Planned Unit Development (PUD)?

opts.A: Each lot must be identical in size and shape
opts.B: Mixed land uses and flexible design standards within a single development
opts.C: Only single-family homes may be built
opts.D: It is exempt from all zoning regulations

questions.exp: A PUD allows a developer to mix residential types, commercial uses, and open space within one project, often with more flexible design standards than standard zoning, in exchange for overall community benefits.

questions.q: Federal law requires sellers of homes built before 1978 to disclose the presence of known:

opts.A: Radon gas
opts.B: Underground storage tanks
opts.C: Lead-based paint
opts.D: Asbestos insulation

questions.exp: The Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act (1992) requires disclosure of known LBP hazards in housing built before 1978, when LBP was banned for residential use. Buyers get 10 days to test.

questions.q: The EPA's recommended action level for radon gas in a home is:

opts.A: 2 pCi/L
opts.B: 4 pCi/L
opts.C: 10 pCi/L
opts.D: 0.4 pCi/L

questions.exp: The EPA recommends mitigation when indoor radon levels reach or exceed 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L). Radon is a colorless, odorless radioactive gas that is the second leading cause of lung cancer in the U.S.

questions.q: Asbestos is considered most dangerous when it is:

opts.A: Intact and undisturbed in good condition (non-friable)
opts.B: Encapsulated with a sealant coating
opts.C: Located in exterior siding
opts.D: Friable — crumbling and releasing fibers into the air

questions.exp: Friable asbestos (easily crumbled by hand) releases microscopic fibers that can be inhaled, causing mesothelioma and lung cancer. Non-friable, well-bonded asbestos in good condition is often safely left in place.

questions.q: The federal law establishing a Superfund to clean up contaminated sites is:

opts.A: RESPA
opts.B: CERCLA
opts.C: TILA
opts.D: FIRREA

questions.exp: CERCLA (Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act, 1980) created the Superfund program. It holds past and present owners, operators, and generators potentially liable for cleanup costs.

questions.q: A real estate agent notices an underground storage tank on a commercial property she is listing. She should FIRST:

opts.A: Remove the tank immediately
opts.B: Ignore it if the seller says it is no longer in use
opts.C: List the property without mentioning the tank
opts.D: Disclose its presence and recommend an environmental assessment

questions.exp: USTs — especially older ones — may leak petroleum products into the soil and groundwater. A licensee must disclose known material defects (including environmental hazards) and should recommend a Phase I/II environmental assessment.

questions.q: Wetlands are regulated primarily under which federal law?

opts.A: Section 404 of the Clean Water Act
opts.B: RESPA
opts.C: CERCLA
opts.D: The Fair Housing Act

questions.exp: Section 404 of the Clean Water Act requires a permit from the Army Corps of Engineers before dredging or filling wetlands. Wetlands provide flood control, water filtration, and wildlife habitat.

questions.q: A property owner unknowingly purchases a commercial site with soil contamination from a prior industrial use. Under CERCLA, the owner may be held:

opts.A: Potentially liable as a current owner, even without knowledge
opts.B: Responsible only if they were the original polluter
opts.C: Exempt because they did not cause the contamination
opts.D: Liable only after the government gives 30 days' notice

questions.exp: CERCLA imposes strict, joint, and several liability on current owners, past owners, generators, and transporters — regardless of fault. An "innocent landowner" defense is narrow and requires due diligence (Phase I assessment).

questions.q: Formerly contaminated industrial sites that have been remediated and returned to productive use are called:

opts.A: Greenbelt areas
opts.B: Superfund sites
opts.C: Brownfields
opts.D: Buffer zones

questions.exp: Brownfields are previously developed (often industrial or commercial) sites with known or suspected contamination. Federal and state programs encourage cleanup and redevelopment through grants and liability protections.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide is BEST described as:

opts.A: A colorless, odorless, potentially deadly gas produced by incomplete combustion
opts.B: A visible yellow-green gas with a strong odor
opts.C: A radioactive gas that rises from soil
opts.D: A fiber released from deteriorating building materials

questions.exp: CO is produced by fuel-burning appliances (furnaces, water heaters, stoves). It is undetectable without a CO detector. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, and in severe cases, death.

questions.q: Mold growth in a house is MOST commonly associated with:

opts.A: Elevated radon levels
opts.B: Proximity to power lines
opts.C: Moisture intrusion and poor ventilation
opts.D: Old lead-based paint

questions.exp: Mold requires moisture (leaks, flooding, condensation) and organic material to grow. Proper ventilation and moisture control are the primary prevention strategies. Some molds produce mycotoxins that are harmful to health.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a material fact that a licensee must disclose to buyers?

opts.A: A known underground storage tank on the property
opts.B: A neighbor's religion
opts.C: The seller is going through a divorce
opts.D: The seller's reason for moving

questions.exp: Material facts are facts that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they'd pay. A UST is a material environmental hazard requiring disclosure. Personal circumstances and protected class information must NOT be disclosed.

questions.q: Electromagnetic fields (EMF) associated with high-voltage power lines are:

opts.A: Proven to cause cancer at all exposure levels
opts.B: Regulated under CERCLA cleanup requirements
opts.C: A stigma issue with uncertain health effects that may affect property value
opts.D: Irrelevant to real estate transactions

questions.exp: EMF's health effects are scientifically debated, but proximity to high-voltage lines can stigmatize property and affect value. Licensees should disclose proximity to power lines as a potential concern.

questions.q: A Phase I Environmental Site Assessment is designed to:

opts.A: Test soil and groundwater samples for contamination
opts.B: Identify potential contamination through records review and site inspection without testing
opts.C: Remove any contamination found on the site
opts.D: Certify a property as free from all environmental hazards

questions.exp: Phase I = non-intrusive records review, interviews, and visual inspection to identify recognized environmental conditions (RECs). Phase II involves actual sampling and testing. Neither certifies a property as clean.

questions.q: The primary health risk associated with exposure to lead-based paint dust is:

opts.A: Respiratory disease in adults
opts.B: Skin irritation and rashes
opts.C: Liver disease in elderly individuals
opts.D: Neurological damage, especially in young children

questions.exp: Lead poisoning in children causes irreversible neurological damage (learning disabilities, lowered IQ, behavioral problems). Children under 6 are most vulnerable because they put hands and objects in their mouths.

questions.q: A leaking underground storage tank (LUST) containing petroleum products is regulated under:

opts.A: RCRA (Resource Conservation and Recovery Act)
opts.B: CERCLA only
opts.C: The Fair Housing Act
opts.D: RESPA

questions.exp: RCRA regulates the management of hazardous and non-hazardous solid waste, including underground storage tanks. The EPA's UST program under RCRA sets standards for tank design, installation, detection, and corrective action.

questions.q: A seller of a pre-1978 home must give the buyer how many days to conduct a lead-based paint inspection?

opts.A: 3 days
opts.B: 10 days
opts.C: 7 days
opts.D: 30 days

questions.exp: Federal law provides buyers of pre-1978 homes a 10-day window to conduct a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment at their own expense. Buyers may waive this right in writing.

questions.q: Urea-formaldehyde foam insulation was commonly used in homes during the 1970s. Its MAIN health concern is:

opts.A: It causes lead poisoning
opts.B: It releases radon gas
opts.C: Off-gassing of formaldehyde vapors that irritate respiratory systems
opts.D: It contains asbestos fibers

questions.exp: UFFI releases formaldehyde vapor (off-gassing), which can cause eye, nose, and throat irritation and has been linked to cancer. The EPA banned UFFI in 1982; homes with it in good condition may have low emissions today.

questions.q: Which action BEST reduces the risk of radon exposure in a home?

opts.A: Encapsulating the basement walls with lead paint
opts.B: Sub-slab depressurization (soil suction) mitigation system
opts.C: Installing a carbon monoxide detector
opts.D: Replacing lead pipes with copper plumbing

questions.exp: The most effective and common radon mitigation technique is sub-slab depressurization — a pipe and fan system that draws radon from beneath the slab and vents it outside before it can enter the living space.

questions.q: A real estate licensee learns that a property was the site of a murder three years ago. In Pennsylvania, must this be disclosed?

opts.A: Yes, always — it is a material fact
opts.B: Yes, but only if the buyer specifically asks
opts.C: Yes, within 30 days of listing
opts.D: No — PA law does not require disclosure of psychological stigma

questions.exp: Pennsylvania's seller disclosure law focuses on physical conditions. Psychological stigma (deaths, hauntings, crimes) are generally not required to be disclosed unless the seller volunteers the information. Licensees should avoid making false statements but are not obligated to reveal stigma.

questions.q: Which federal agency sets and enforces standards for the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP)?

opts.A: EPA
opts.B: HUD
opts.C: Army Corps of Engineers
opts.D: FEMA

questions.exp: The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) administers the NFIP. Flood insurance is required for federally backed loans on properties in Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHA) mapped by FEMA.

questions.q: The oldest and most common method of legal description in the eastern United States, which traces the boundary of a parcel using compass bearings and distances, is called:

opts.A: Lot and block
opts.B: Metes and bounds
opts.C: Rectangular (government) survey
opts.D: Datum and benchmark

questions.exp: Metes and bounds describes land by starting at a point of beginning (POB), then tracing boundaries using bearings (compass directions) and distances (metes) and physical monuments or reference points (bounds). It closes back at the POB.

questions.q: In the rectangular (government) survey system, a township contains how many sections?
questions.exp: A township is a 6-mile × 6-mile square containing 36 sections, each 1 mile × 1 mile (640 acres). Sections are numbered 1–36, starting in the northeast corner and snaking back and forth.

questions.q: One section of land in the rectangular survey system contains:

opts.A: 160 acres
opts.B: 320 acres
opts.C: 1,280 acres
opts.D: 640 acres

questions.exp: One section = 1 square mile = 640 acres. A half-section = 320 acres; a quarter-section = 160 acres; a quarter-quarter section = 40 acres (the smallest standard rectangular survey unit).

questions.q: A property is described as "the NW¼ of the SE¼ of Section 12, T3N, R2W." How many acres does this parcel contain?

opts.A: 40 acres
opts.B: 160 acres
opts.C: 80 acres
opts.D: 640 acres

questions.exp: SE¼ of Section 12 = 160 acres. NW¼ of that 160 acres = 40 acres. The formula: 640 ÷ 4 ÷ 4 = 40 acres.

questions.q: The simplest legal description method — used in platted subdivisions — is:

opts.A: Metes and bounds
opts.B: Lot and block
opts.C: Rectangular survey
opts.D: Datum and elevation

questions.exp: The lot-and-block (recorded plat) method describes property by reference to a recorded subdivision map: "Lot 14, Block 3, Sunny Acres Subdivision, recorded in Plat Book 22, Page 41, Luzerne County, PA."

questions.q: The starting point of a metes and bounds description is called the:

opts.A: Point of beginning (POB)
opts.B: Benchmark
opts.C: Principal meridian
opts.D: Baseline

questions.exp: Every metes and bounds description starts and ends at the same POB — a fixed monument or legally defined reference point. The description must close (return to the POB) to be valid.

questions.q: A datum is BEST defined as:

opts.A: A compass bearing used in metes and bounds
opts.B: A permanent marker showing elevation
opts.C: A recorded subdivision plat
opts.D: A base plane from which elevations are measured

questions.exp: A datum is a reference plane (often mean sea level) used for measuring elevations. A benchmark is a physical marker showing a known elevation based on the datum — used in surveys to establish height references.

questions.q: In the rectangular survey system, the north-south reference lines are called:

opts.A: Principal meridians
opts.B: Baselines
opts.C: Range lines
opts.D: Township lines

questions.exp: Principal meridians run north-south; baselines run east-west. Range lines (parallel to the meridian) and township lines (parallel to the baseline) create the grid of 6-mile squares called townships.

questions.q: A legal description must always be sufficient to:

opts.A: Include the purchase price of the property
opts.B: List all improvements on the property
opts.C: Identify and locate the exact parcel of land
opts.D: Match the county tax parcel number

questions.exp: A legal description must uniquely and precisely identify a parcel of land so it can be located on the ground. A street address alone is NOT a legal description and is insufficient for a deed or mortgage.

questions.q: A property is described as Section 6, Township 4 North, Range 3 West. The "4 North" refers to:

opts.A: The section number within the township
opts.B: The range east of the principal meridian
opts.C: The township's position north of the baseline
opts.D: The number of acres in the north portion

questions.exp: "T4N" means the township is 4 rows north of the baseline. "R3W" means 3 columns west of the principal meridian. Together they pinpoint one 36-square-mile township in the rectangular survey grid.

questions.q: Which method of legal description would MOST likely be used for a property in an older Pennsylvania city with irregular street layouts?

opts.A: Rectangular survey
opts.B: Lot and block
opts.C: Metes and bounds
opts.D: ALTA survey with datum

questions.exp: The rectangular survey system was used mainly in states west of Ohio. Pennsylvania, being an original colony, relies on metes and bounds (and lot-and-block for platted subdivisions). Rectangular survey is rarely used in PA.

questions.q: A deed contains only the street address and no other property identification. This deed is likely:

opts.A: Valid because the address is sufficient identification
opts.B: Valid if the county tax ID number is also included
opts.C: Valid if the buyer and seller both sign it
opts.D: Deficient — a street address is not a legal description

questions.exp: A deed must contain a legal description sufficient to locate the property. A street address can change and does not uniquely identify a parcel. Without a proper legal description, the deed may be unenforceable.

questions.q: A township in the rectangular survey system is a square that measures:

opts.A: 1 mile × 1 mile
opts.B: 3 miles × 3 miles
opts.C: 6 miles × 6 miles
opts.D: 10 miles × 10 miles

questions.exp: A township = 6 × 6 miles = 36 square miles. It contains 36 sections (each 1 square mile). The term "township" in legal description should not be confused with a political township (municipality).

questions.q: When a metes and bounds description refers to a "monument," it means:

opts.A: A historic landmark
opts.B: A physical object (iron pin, tree, rock) used as a boundary reference point
opts.C: A benchmark elevation marker
opts.D: A recorded plat

questions.exp: Monuments are physical objects — natural (streams, trees, boulders) or artificial (iron pins, concrete posts) — placed at corners and boundaries to mark the land described in a metes and bounds description.

questions.q: Section 1 of a township is located in which corner?

opts.A: Southwest corner
opts.B: Northwest corner
opts.C: Southeast corner
opts.D: Northeast corner

questions.exp: In the rectangular survey system, Section 1 is in the northeast corner of a township. Numbering proceeds west to Section 6, then drops south to Section 7 in the east, continuing in a boustrophedon (serpentine) pattern, ending at Section 36 in the southeast.

questions.q: The NE¼ of a section contains how many acres?

opts.A: 40 acres
opts.B: 160 acres
opts.C: 80 acres
opts.D: 320 acres

questions.exp: One section = 640 acres. One quarter of 640 = 160 acres. The NE¼, NW¼, SE¼, and SW¼ each contain 160 acres, equal to a classic homestead quarter-section.

questions.q: A developer records a subdivision plat showing Lot 5, Block B. When a buyer purchases this lot, the legal description in the deed will reference:

opts.A: The lot and block number from the recorded plat
opts.B: The rectangular survey coordinates
opts.C: The metes and bounds of Lot 5 only
opts.D: The county tax parcel number

questions.exp: Once a plat is recorded, each lot can be described simply by its lot number, block number, subdivision name, and recording reference. The deed incorporates the plat by reference.

questions.q: Which type of survey provides the most comprehensive information, including improvements, easements, and encroachments?

opts.A: Topographic survey
opts.B: Subdivision survey
opts.C: Boundary survey
opts.D: ALTA/NSPS survey

questions.exp: An ALTA/NSPS (American Land Title Association / National Society of Professional Surveyors) survey is the most comprehensive — required by lenders and title insurers on commercial transactions — and locates all improvements, encroachments, easements, and utilities.

questions.q: A buyer's lender requires a survey before closing to confirm that a neighbor's fence is not encroaching on the property. This type of boundary survey locates:

opts.A: Underground utilities only
opts.B: The exact boundaries and any encroachments
opts.C: All improvements within 100 feet of the property
opts.D: The elevation of the property relative to flood zones

questions.exp: A boundary survey locates the legal boundaries of a parcel and identifies encroachments (a neighbor's fence, driveway, or building crossing the property line). It is based on the legal description in the deed.

questions.q: In a rectangular survey description, "T2S, R4E" means the property is located:

opts.A: 2 townships east and 4 ranges south of the intersection
opts.B: 4 ranges east and 2 townships north
opts.C: 2 townships south of the baseline and 4 ranges east of the principal meridian
opts.D: Section 2, 4th tier east of the meridian

questions.exp: T2S = 2 township rows south of the baseline; R4E = 4 range columns east of the principal meridian. The intersection of this township row and range column identifies the township square.

questions.q: The highest form of property ownership, with no restrictions on duration, is:

opts.A: Life estate
opts.B: Fee simple defeasible
opts.C: Fee simple absolute
opts.D: Leasehold estate

questions.exp: Fee simple absolute (fee simple) is the most complete ownership — unlimited duration, freely transferable, devisable, inheritable, with no conditions. It is the "highest" freehold estate recognized by law.

questions.q: A grantor deeds property "to the City of Scranton, so long as the land is used as a public park." If the city stops using it as a park, ownership returns to:

opts.A: The city keeps it forever
opts.B: The grantor or grantor's heirs (reverter)
opts.C: The state of Pennsylvania
opts.D: The nearest municipality

questions.exp: This is a fee simple determinable — ownership automatically reverts to the grantor (or heirs) if the stated condition is violated. The magic words are "so long as," "while," or "during." Compare to fee simple subject to condition subsequent (grantor must re-enter).

questions.q: A mother conveys her home "to my daughter for life, then to my son." During the daughter's life, she holds a:

opts.A: Fee simple estate
opts.B: Leasehold estate
opts.C: Remainder interest in fee simple
opts.D: Life estate

questions.exp: A life estate grants ownership only for the measuring life (here, the daughter's life). The son holds a remainder interest and receives fee simple ownership when the daughter dies. The daughter cannot convey more than her life estate.

questions.q: An easement that is attached to the land and benefits a neighboring property is called an easement:

opts.A: In gross
opts.B: Appurtenant
opts.C: By necessity
opts.D: By prescription

questions.exp: An easement appurtenant benefits a dominant tenement (the property that uses the easement) and burdens a servient tenement (the property the easement crosses). It runs with the land and transfers with both properties.

questions.q: A utility company has the right to run power lines across a homeowner's property. This is an example of an easement:

opts.A: In gross
opts.B: By necessity
opts.C: Appurtenant
opts.D: By prescription

questions.exp: A commercial easement in gross benefits a person or entity (not a neighboring parcel). Utility easements, pipeline rights-of-way, and railroad rights-of-way are classic easements in gross. There is no dominant tenement.

questions.q: A landowner gains an easement over a neighbor's land by using it openly, continuously, exclusively, and without permission for 21 years. This is an easement:

opts.A: Appurtenant
opts.B: By necessity
opts.C: In gross
opts.D: By prescription

questions.exp: A prescriptive easement is acquired through hostile, open, actual, continuous, exclusive use for the statutory period (varies by state). It is similar to adverse possession but results in an easement right, not full ownership.

questions.q: A landowner whose property is completely surrounded by other properties has a legal right of access across a neighbor's land through an easement:

opts.A: In gross
opts.B: By necessity
opts.C: By prescription
opts.D: Appurtenant created by express grant

questions.exp: An easement by necessity is implied by law when a parcel is landlocked — completely enclosed by other property with no access to a public road. Courts recognize this right because property is useless without access.

questions.q: A neighbor's fence encroaches 18 inches over the property line onto the owner's land. This is called:

opts.A: An easement appurtenant
opts.B: A license
opts.C: An encroachment
opts.D: A deed restriction

questions.exp: An encroachment is the physical intrusion of a structure, improvement, or tree from one property onto another. It is discoverable by survey and may become a prescriptive easement if the statutory period passes without objection.

questions.q: Permission given to a person to use land for a specific purpose that is revocable at will and does NOT create an interest in land is called:

opts.A: A license
opts.B: A lease
opts.C: An easement
opts.D: A deed restriction

questions.exp: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use someone's land (e.g., a ticket to a sports event, permission to fish in a pond). It is NOT an interest in real property and cannot be assigned or inherited.

questions.q: A life tenant who owns a life estate may NOT:

opts.A: Occupy and use the property during her lifetime
opts.B: Lease the property to tenants during her lifetime
opts.C: Will the property to her children in fee simple
opts.D: Mortgage the property during her lifetime

questions.exp: A life tenant can only convey what they own — a life estate measured by their own life. They cannot convey more than they have; therefore, they cannot will fee simple ownership. The remainder interest goes to the remainderman named in the original deed.

questions.q: Which of the following is a leasehold estate?

opts.A: Fee simple absolute
opts.B: Life estate
opts.C: Fee simple determinable
opts.D: Tenancy for years

questions.exp: Leasehold estates (less-than-freehold) include: tenancy for years (fixed term), tenancy at will (no fixed term), tenancy from period-to-period (month-to-month), and tenancy at sufferance (holdover). All others listed are freehold estates.

questions.q: An easement appurtenant requires:

opts.A: One parcel of land only
opts.B: Court approval to be valid
opts.C: A minimum of 21 years of use
opts.D: Two parcels — a dominant and a servient tenement

questions.exp: An easement appurtenant needs exactly two adjacent (or nearby) parcels: the dominant tenement (benefited land) and the servient tenement (burdened land). Without a dominant estate, there can be no easement appurtenant.

questions.q: The homestead exemption in Pennsylvania protects:

opts.A: A home from all creditors indefinitely
opts.B: A home from property taxes entirely
opts.C: A portion of assessed value from property taxes for owner-occupants
opts.D: A home from being condemned by eminent domain

questions.exp: Pennsylvania's homestead exclusion reduces the assessed value subject to school property taxes for owner-occupied primary residences. It does not protect against all creditors (unlike some states' homestead laws).

questions.q: A property owner "pur autre vie" holds a life estate measured by:

opts.A: The owner's own lifespan
opts.B: The life of a third person
opts.C: A fixed term of 99 years
opts.D: The duration of a lease agreement

questions.exp: "Pur autre vie" (French: "for another's life") means the life estate is measured by someone other than the holder. Example: A conveys to B "for the life of C." B owns the estate until C dies, even if B dies first (in which case B's heirs hold it until C dies).

questions.q: Which of the following would TERMINATE an easement appurtenant?

opts.A: Merger — when the same person acquires both the dominant and servient properties
opts.B: The easement holder's death
opts.C: Sale of the dominant tenement to a new owner
opts.D: Nonuse for one year

questions.exp: Merger extinguishes an easement because you cannot have an easement on your own land. Other termination methods include written release, abandonment (acts showing intent to abandon), and condemnation of the servient estate.

questions.q: A deed restriction states that the property may only be used for residential purposes. A buyer wants to open a dental office there. The buyer:

opts.A: Cannot open the dental office because the deed restriction controls
opts.B: Can proceed after obtaining a variance
opts.C: Can proceed if local zoning allows commercial use
opts.D: Can proceed because deed restrictions expire after 25 years in PA

questions.exp: Deed restrictions (private controls) and zoning (public controls) both apply. Even if zoning permits commercial use, the deed restriction prohibiting non-residential use is still enforceable by neighboring property owners.

questions.q: A lien is an example of which type of encumbrance?

opts.A: Easement
opts.B: Financial encumbrance
opts.C: Deed restriction
opts.D: Physical encroachment

questions.exp: Encumbrances on property are categorized as financial (liens — mortgage, tax lien, mechanic's lien) or non-financial (easements, deed restrictions, encroachments). Liens affect the owner's financial interest but not the physical use.

questions.q: A seller has a mortgage, a home equity loan, and a mechanic's lien on her property. These are all examples of:

opts.A: Specific liens
opts.B: Deed restrictions
opts.C: Easements in gross
opts.D: General liens

questions.exp: A specific lien attaches to a specific property only (mortgage, mechanic's lien, property tax lien). A general lien attaches to all property owned by the debtor (judgment lien, IRS lien). Mortgages and mechanic's liens are specific.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a way to create an easement?

opts.A: Express grant (written agreement)
opts.B: Implication (necessity)
opts.C: Oral permission revocable at will
opts.D: Prescription (long-term use)

questions.exp: Oral revocable permission creates only a license, not an easement. Easements are created by express grant (deed/contract), implication (necessity, prior use), prescription (hostile use over time), or condemnation.

questions.q: A life tenant is required to:

opts.A: Pay off all mortgages before the remainderman takes title
opts.B: Improve the property for the benefit of the remainderman
opts.C: Transfer ownership to the remainderman upon request
opts.D: Avoid waste — not damage or diminish the value of the property

questions.exp: The doctrine of waste prohibits a life tenant from damaging, destroying, or substantially diminishing the value of the property in a way that harms the remainderman's future interest. The life tenant must maintain the property in good condition.

questions.q: Two friends purchase a vacation cabin together, each owning a 50% undivided interest. Either can sell their share to a third party without the other's consent. They hold title as:

opts.A: Tenants in common
opts.B: Tenants by the entirety
opts.C: Joint tenants
opts.D: Community property owners

questions.exp: Tenancy in common: each co-owner holds an undivided interest that is freely transferable, inheritable, and devisable — no right of survivorship. Shares need not be equal. Any co-owner may sell or mortgage their interest without the others' consent.

questions.q: Joint tenancy requires four unities. Which of the following is NOT one of them?

opts.A: Unity of purpose
opts.B: Unity of title
opts.C: Unity of time
opts.D: Unity of possession

questions.exp: The four unities of joint tenancy (TTIP): Time (acquired simultaneously), Title (same deed/instrument), Interest (equal shares), Possession (same right to possess the whole). "Unity of purpose" is not one of them.

questions.q: If one joint tenant sells their interest to a third party, the third party takes title as:

opts.A: A joint tenant with the remaining owners
opts.B: A tenant in common with the remaining owners
opts.C: A tenant by the entirety
opts.D: A life tenant

questions.exp: When a joint tenant conveys their interest, the four unities (especially time and title) are broken for that share. The buyer becomes a tenant in common with the remaining joint tenants (who may still be joint tenants among themselves).

questions.q: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of ownership available ONLY to:

opts.A: Business partners
opts.B: Any two related individuals
opts.C: Legally married spouses
opts.D: Co-owners of commercial property

questions.exp: Tenancy by the entirety treats the married couple as one legal entity. It includes right of survivorship, and neither spouse can convey or encumber their interest alone without the other's consent — a strong creditor protection in PA.

questions.q: In a condominium, each owner holds fee simple title to their individual unit and also owns:

opts.A: The entire building in joint tenancy
opts.B: Stock in the condominium corporation
opts.C: An undivided interest in the common elements
opts.D: A proprietary lease on the common areas

questions.exp: Condominium ownership = fee simple to the unit + an undivided percentage interest in common elements (hallways, roof, land, recreation areas) as a tenant in common with all other unit owners.

questions.q: In a cooperative (co-op), residents own:

opts.A: Shares of stock in the cooperative corporation plus a proprietary lease
opts.B: An undivided interest in the common elements
opts.C: Fee simple title to their individual units
opts.D: A life estate in their apartment unit

questions.exp: Cooperative ownership is personal property (stock + proprietary lease), not real property. The corporation owns the building; residents are shareholders who lease their units. Selling requires board approval in most co-ops.

questions.q: Which characteristic distinguishes joint tenancy from tenancy in common?

opts.A: Joint tenancy includes the right of survivorship
opts.B: Tenants in common may not sell their interest without consent
opts.C: Joint tenants may hold unequal shares
opts.D: Tenancy in common requires four unities

questions.exp: Right of survivorship is the defining feature of joint tenancy — when a joint tenant dies, their interest automatically passes to the surviving joint tenants, bypassing the will and probate. Tenancy in common has no survivorship right.

questions.q: Ownership of property by one person or entity alone is called:

opts.A: Tenancy in common
opts.B: Joint tenancy
opts.C: Tenancy by the entirety
opts.D: Tenancy in severalty

questions.exp: Tenancy in severalty (ownership in severalty) means sole ownership by one person or legal entity. "Severalty" refers to ownership being severed from others — held alone. The word does not refer to "several" owners.

questions.q: A time-share owner typically holds:

opts.A: Fee simple absolute to the unit in perpetuity
opts.B: An interval ownership or right-to-use interest for specified time periods
opts.C: A tenancy in common with right of survivorship
opts.D: A cooperative share in the resort corporation

questions.exp: Time-shares may be structured as interval ownership (actual fee simple for a specified time period each year) or right-to-use (a contractual right to use the unit for specified periods, not ownership). Both are governed by PA's Time-Share Act.

questions.q: A married couple holds title to their home as tenants by the entirety. If the husband incurs a judgment lien for a personal debt, the lien:

opts.A: Immediately attaches to the home
opts.B: Attaches to the husband's half only
opts.C: Cannot attach to the property without both spouses' consent
opts.D: Forces immediate sale of the home

questions.exp: Tenancy by the entirety provides protection from one spouse's individual creditors — neither spouse can encumber the property individually. The lien cannot attach unless the debt is a joint obligation of both spouses.

questions.q: A planned unit development (PUD) homeowner typically owns:

opts.A: Only the interior of the unit; the corporation owns the structure
opts.B: Stock in the PUD association
opts.C: Fee simple title to their lot and home, plus membership in an HOA that manages common areas
opts.D: An undivided interest in the entire development

questions.exp: Unlike a condo (unit only) or co-op (stock), a PUD homeowner owns their lot and structure outright (fee simple). Common areas are owned and maintained by a mandatory homeowners association (HOA) funded by dues.

questions.q: Which statement about condominiums is TRUE?

opts.A: The condominium association owns the individual units
opts.B: Owners may not obtain individual financing (mortgages) on their units
opts.C: Common areas are owned equally by all owners in joint tenancy
opts.D: Each unit owner is responsible for paying their own real estate taxes on their unit

questions.exp: Each condo unit is a separate taxable parcel with its own deed and tax bill. Owners get individual mortgages. Common areas are owned as tenants in common (not joint tenancy). The association manages but does not own units.

questions.q: A tenancy in common can be terminated by a legal action to divide the property called:

opts.A: Condemnation
opts.B: Quiet title
opts.C: Escheat
opts.D: Partition

questions.exp: Partition is a court action that divides co-owned property into separate parcels (partition in kind) or, if physical division is impractical, forces a sale and divides the proceeds (partition by sale). Any co-tenant may bring a partition action.

questions.q: Community property is a form of co-ownership between spouses that exists in:

opts.A: All 50 states
opts.B: Pennsylvania specifically
opts.C: Approximately 9 western and southwestern states
opts.D: Only states that have abolished tenancy by the entirety

questions.exp: Community property states (AZ, CA, ID, LA, NV, NM, TX, WA, WI) treat most property acquired during marriage as equally owned by both spouses. Pennsylvania is NOT a community property state — it uses common law ownership rules.

questions.q: In a cooperative building, a resident who wants to sell their apartment must typically:

opts.A: Simply record a new deed like any other sale
opts.B: Obtain approval from the cooperative board
opts.C: Pay a transfer tax to the cooperative corporation
opts.D: Convert their shares to a condominium unit first

questions.exp: Because the co-op corporation owns the building, it has the right to approve or reject prospective purchasers of shares (within fair housing limits). Board approval is a significant feature that distinguishes co-ops from condos.

questions.q: Two joint tenants, A and B, own a property. A dies. What happens to A's interest?

opts.A: A's heirs inherit A's 50% share as tenants in common with B
opts.B: The property must be sold and proceeds divided equally
opts.C: The state acquires A's half through escheat
opts.D: B automatically becomes the sole owner through right of survivorship

questions.exp: Right of survivorship is the defining characteristic of joint tenancy. Upon A's death, A's interest instantly and automatically passes to B — it does not pass through A's will or probate. B now owns 100% in severalty.

questions.q: An owner of a condominium unit defaults on their mortgage. The lender may foreclose on:

opts.A: The entire condominium building
opts.B: The individual unit only
opts.C: All common elements
opts.D: The owner's interest in the HOA

questions.exp: Each condo unit is an independent real estate parcel with its own deed and mortgage. Foreclosure on one unit does not affect other owners. The lender's lien and foreclosure are limited to the defaulting unit.

questions.q: A trust in which the beneficiary's identity is kept private and the trustee holds title to real property is called a:

opts.A: Land trust (Illinois-type land trust)
opts.B: General partnership
opts.C: Tenancy in common
opts.D: Real estate investment trust (REIT)

questions.exp: A land trust (used in IL and some other states) holds title to real property with the trustee named on the deed, keeping the beneficiary's identity off public records. REITs are investment vehicles traded on stock exchanges.

questions.q: Which form of ownership provides the most protection to a married couple from the individual debts of one spouse?

opts.A: Tenancy in common
opts.B: Tenancy by the entirety
opts.C: Joint tenancy
opts.D: Tenancy in severalty

questions.exp: Tenancy by the entirety (available to married couples in PA) prevents either spouse's individual creditors from attaching the property — providing the strongest creditor protection of any co-ownership form.

questions.q: A real estate investment trust (REIT) allows investors to:

opts.A: Own real property directly in joint tenancy
opts.B: Receive tenancy in common rights in commercial buildings
opts.C: Claim homestead exemptions on invested properties
opts.D: Invest in a portfolio of real estate assets through publicly traded shares

questions.exp: REITs are companies that own income-producing real estate, traded on stock exchanges. Investors buy shares (personal property, not real property). REITs must distribute at least 90% of taxable income to shareholders as dividends.

questions.q: Property taxes based on the assessed value of real estate are called:

opts.A: Special assessments
opts.B: Ad valorem taxes
opts.C: Transfer taxes
opts.D: Excise taxes

questions.exp: Ad valorem (Latin: "according to value") taxes are levied based on property value. The local government assesses each property and applies a tax rate (mill rate) to determine the annual tax bill.

questions.q: A property is assessed at $180,000 and the local tax rate is 25 mills. The annual property tax is:
A special assessment is BEST described as:

opts.A: A charge levied on properties that benefit from a specific public improvement
opts.B: A penalty tax on properties with code violations
opts.C: An increase in ad valorem taxes caused by rising property values
opts.D: A tax on income earned from rental properties

questions.exp: Special assessments (e.g., for new sidewalks, water/sewer lines, or street paving) are charged only to properties that directly benefit from the improvement — not all properties in the jurisdiction.

questions.q: Which type of lien applies to ALL property owned by the debtor?

opts.A: Mortgage lien
opts.B: Mechanic's lien
opts.C: Judgment lien
opts.D: Property tax lien

questions.exp: A judgment lien is a general lien that attaches to all real and personal property owned by the debtor in the county where the judgment is recorded. Mortgage, mechanic's, and tax liens are specific liens on a particular property.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, a contractor who was not paid for work performed on a property must file a mechanic's lien claim within:

opts.A: 30 days of completing work
opts.B: 90 days of completing work
opts.C: 2 years of completing work
opts.D: 6 months of completing work

questions.exp: Under Pennsylvania's Mechanics' Lien Law, a contractor (or subcontractor) must file a lien claim within 6 months of completing work to preserve their right to collect. Filing after the deadline extinguishes the lien right.

questions.q: Which lien generally has the HIGHEST priority in a foreclosure sale?

opts.A: Real property tax lien
opts.B: Mechanic's lien
opts.C: First mortgage lien
opts.D: Judgment lien

questions.exp: Real property tax liens have "super priority" — they are paid first before all other liens, regardless of when the other liens were recorded. After taxes are paid, liens are satisfied in order of their recording date (first in time, first in right).

questions.q: A lis pendens is:

opts.A: A tax lien filed by the IRS
opts.B: A notice of pending litigation affecting title to property
opts.C: A mechanic's lien for unpaid construction work
opts.D: A special assessment for street improvements

questions.exp: Lis pendens (Latin: "suit pending") is recorded in the public record to notify prospective buyers and lenders that the title to the property is the subject of an ongoing lawsuit. A buyer who purchases with a lis pendens on record takes subject to the outcome of that litigation.

questions.q: An owner's property is assessed at $220,000 but the owner believes the actual market value is $180,000. The owner should:

opts.A: Refuse to pay the tax bill
opts.B: File an appeal with the local board of assessment appeals
opts.C: File a mechanic's lien against the county
opts.D: Petition the zoning board for a variance

questions.exp: Property owners who believe their assessment is incorrect may appeal to the local Board of Assessment Appeals (or Assessment Review Board). If unsuccessful, they may appeal further to the Court of Common Pleas.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Realty Transfer Tax is typically paid by:

opts.A: The buyer only
opts.B: The lender only
opts.C: Only when the property is a commercial transaction
opts.D: Both the buyer and seller, as negotiated

questions.exp: PA imposes a 1% state transfer tax + a local (municipal/school) transfer tax (typically 1%) = approximately 2% total. By custom, buyer and seller typically split the tax equally, though it is negotiable.

questions.q: A subcontractor who was not paid by the general contractor (not the property owner) may file a mechanic's lien against the property. This is TRUE because:

opts.A: Subcontractors have superior rights over property owners
opts.B: PA mechanics' lien law extends rights to subcontractors who provided work or materials
opts.C: Pennsylvania law allows subcontractors to lien only if they give proper preliminary notice
opts.D: Subcontractors must first sue the general contractor and obtain a judgment

questions.exp: In Pennsylvania, both contractors and subcontractors (and material suppliers) may file mechanic's liens against the improved property, even if the owner paid the general contractor in full — as long as proper notice (120-day preliminary notice for subs) was given.

questions.q: An equalization factor (assessment ratio) is used to:

opts.A: Bring assessed values into line with current market values
opts.B: Determine the highest and best use of a property
opts.C: Set a uniform mill rate across all properties in a county
opts.D: Calculate special assessment amounts for public improvements

questions.exp: When assessed values across a county fall behind actual market values, an equalization factor (multiplier) is applied to adjust them for fairness — ensuring property owners throughout the jurisdiction are taxed equitably.

questions.q: When a property is sold to satisfy unpaid taxes, the former owner may have a right to recover the property by paying all taxes, interest, and costs. This right is called:

opts.A: Right of first refusal
opts.B: Redemption right before the tax sale
opts.C: Statutory right of redemption
opts.D: Equitable redemption

questions.exp: The statutory right of redemption (post-sale redemption) allows a former owner to reclaim property after a tax sale by paying all outstanding taxes, penalties, interest, and costs within a statutory period set by state law.

questions.q: A federal tax lien filed by the IRS against a taxpayer is an example of a:

opts.A: Specific lien
opts.B: Voluntary lien
opts.C: Mechanic's lien
opts.D: General involuntary lien

questions.exp: The IRS federal tax lien is a general lien (attaches to all property) and involuntary (imposed by law without the owner's consent). Mortgages are voluntary specific liens; mechanic's liens are involuntary specific liens.

questions.q: A homeowner's exemption (homestead exemption) in Pennsylvania reduces:

opts.A: The mortgage interest rate
opts.B: The assessed value subject to school property taxes
opts.C: The transfer tax on sale
opts.D: The amount owed on a mechanic's lien

questions.exp: PA's homestead exclusion (under Act 50) allows qualifying owner-occupants to reduce the assessed value used to calculate school property taxes — providing tax relief to primary residence owners.

questions.q: A subordination agreement allows:

opts.A: A lender to increase the interest rate after default
opts.B: A tenant to sublease without landlord approval
opts.C: A lien that is higher in priority to be placed in a lower priority position
opts.D: An owner to reduce property taxes by appealing to the county

questions.exp: A subordination agreement voluntarily changes the priority of liens. For example, a first mortgage lender may agree to subordinate their lien to a new construction loan to facilitate development financing.

questions.q: Which of the following is a VOLUNTARY lien?

opts.A: Mortgage lien
opts.B: Property tax lien
opts.C: Judgment lien
opts.D: Mechanic's lien

questions.exp: A mortgage lien is voluntary — the property owner intentionally grants it as security for a loan. Judgment liens, tax liens, and mechanic's liens are involuntary — imposed without the owner's direct consent.

questions.q: The assessed value of a property is $150,000. The assessment ratio in the county is 60%. What is the estimated market value?
questions.exp: Assessed value ÷ assessment ratio = market value. $150,000 ÷ 0.60 = $250,000. Alternatively: if the county assesses at 60% of market value, market value = assessed value × (1 ÷ 0.60).

questions.q: After a foreclosure sale, surplus funds (proceeds exceeding the debt) are distributed FIRST to:

opts.A: The foreclosing lender
opts.B: The real estate agent who listed the property
opts.C: The county treasurer
opts.D: Junior lien holders in order of priority

questions.exp: After the foreclosing lender (and costs) are paid in full, surplus proceeds go first to other lienholders (in priority order), then to the former property owner. The foreclosing lender receives only what is owed — not excess proceeds.

questions.q: A contractor's lien that is recorded after a first mortgage was recorded will generally be:

opts.A: Superior to the mortgage because contractors have super priority
opts.B: Equal in priority to the mortgage
opts.C: Junior to the mortgage (paid after in foreclosure)
opts.D: Invalid and unenforceable

questions.exp: Priority among voluntary liens follows the "first in time, first in right" rule. A mechanic's lien recorded after a first mortgage is junior to that mortgage. (Exception: in some states, mechanic's liens relate back to when work began.)

questions.q: Pennsylvania imposes a local Earned Income Tax (EIT). For a real estate licensee who is an independent contractor, this tax is paid:

opts.A: By the employing broker on the licensee's behalf
opts.B: Only at year-end with the federal return
opts.C: By the licensee directly to the local taxing authority
opts.D: Through payroll withholding by the broker

questions.exp: Independent contractors receive no payroll withholding — they are responsible for paying their own federal, state, and local taxes (including EIT) directly, typically through quarterly estimated payments.

questions.q: Which type of deed provides the GREATEST protection to a grantee?

opts.A: Quitclaim deed
opts.B: Bargain and sale deed
opts.C: General warranty deed
opts.D: Special warranty deed

questions.exp: A general warranty deed contains six covenants (seisin, quiet enjoyment, further assurance, warranty forever, against encumbrances, and right to convey) covering the entire chain of title — not just the grantor's period of ownership — giving the grantee maximum protection.

questions.q: A deed with the phrase "to have and to hold" is part of which clause?

opts.A: Granting clause
opts.B: Habendum clause
opts.C: Acknowledgment clause
opts.D: Consideration clause

questions.exp: The habendum clause ("to have and to hold") defines the extent of the ownership being transferred. It must be consistent with the granting clause or the granting clause controls.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT required for a deed to be valid?

opts.A: Grantor with legal capacity
opts.B: Granting clause with words of conveyance
opts.C: Adequate description of the property
opts.D: Recording at the county recorder's office

questions.exp: Recording is NOT required for a deed to be legally valid between the parties — it is needed to protect against third parties. The essential elements of a valid deed include grantor, grantee, consideration, legal description, granting clause, and signature of the grantor.

questions.q: A seller conveys title with a special warranty deed. This means the seller warrants the title against defects arising:

opts.A: From any source, ever
opts.B: Before the seller acquired the property
opts.C: Only during the seller's period of ownership
opts.D: Only from the seller's heirs

questions.exp: A special warranty deed limits the seller's warranty to the period during which the seller owned the property. Any defects that existed before the seller took title are not covered.

questions.q: A quitclaim deed conveys:

opts.A: A guaranteed fee simple absolute title
opts.B: Whatever interest the grantor holds, if any, with no warranties
opts.C: Whatever interest the grantee currently holds
opts.D: A life estate in the property

questions.exp: A quitclaim deed transfers only whatever interest the grantor happens to have — which could be nothing. It carries no covenants or warranties whatsoever. It is commonly used to clear clouds on title.

questions.q: Title to real property passes upon death via intestate succession (no will) according to:

opts.A: The decedent's verbal instructions
opts.B: The property's assessed value
opts.C: Pennsylvania's law of descent and distribution
opts.D: The mortgage lender's requirements

questions.exp: When a person dies without a valid will (intestate), Pennsylvania's intestate succession statutes determine how the estate — including real property — passes to heirs. These laws define the priority among surviving spouse, children, and other relatives.

questions.q: Which government power allows the state to take title to property of a person who dies without heirs and without a will?

opts.A: Eminent domain
opts.B: Taxation
opts.C: Escheat
opts.D: Police power

questions.exp: Escheat is the process by which the state acquires title to property of a person who dies intestate with no identifiable heirs. It prevents property from having no legal owner.

questions.q: For a deed to be accepted for recording in Pennsylvania, it must generally include:

opts.A: The grantor's Social Security number
opts.B: The broker's license number
opts.C: A notarized acknowledgment of the grantor's signature
opts.D: The grantee's marital status

questions.exp: Pennsylvania requires that a deed be acknowledged (notarized) before it can be recorded. The notary verifies the grantor's identity and that the signature was made voluntarily.

questions.q: Adverse possession requires all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: Actual, open, and notorious use
opts.B: Continuous use for the statutory period
opts.C: Hostile claim (without owner's permission)
opts.D: Payment of the property's purchase price

questions.exp: Adverse possession requires actual, open, notorious, hostile, exclusive, and continuous use for the statutory period (21 years in Pennsylvania). Payment of a purchase price is never required — adverse possession is a legal doctrine, not a purchase.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, adverse possession generally requires continuous, uninterrupted use for at least:

opts.A: 5 years
opts.B: 21 years
opts.C: 15 years
opts.D: 10 years

questions.exp: Pennsylvania's statute of limitations for adverse possession is 21 years. The claimant must use the property as their own, openly and continuously, without the owner's permission, for the full 21-year period.

questions.q: A patent is a document used to transfer title from:

opts.A: The government to a private individual
opts.B: An estate to the heirs
opts.C: One private party to another
opts.D: A corporation to its shareholders

questions.exp: A patent (also called a land patent or government patent) is the instrument used when the government originally transferred publicly owned land into private ownership. This is the first link in a property's chain of title.

questions.q: A deed must be delivered and accepted to be effective. Delivery is presumed when:

opts.A: The deed is handed to the grantee or placed in escrow
opts.B: The deed is recorded
opts.C: The grantor signs the deed
opts.D: The grantee signs the deed

questions.exp: Delivery means the grantor voluntarily relinquishes control of the deed with the present intent to pass title. Physical delivery to the grantee (or an escrow agent) creates a presumption of delivery. Recording creates an additional presumption but is not the sole test.

questions.q: When real property is transferred by will, the document used is called a:

opts.A: Deed of trust
opts.B: Devise
opts.C: Quitclaim deed
opts.D: Bequest

questions.exp: A devise is the transfer of real property by will. The recipient is called the devisee. A bequest (or legacy) refers to personal property transferred by will. Both are testamentary transfers (via a will).

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes the covenant of "seisin" in a general warranty deed?

opts.A: The grantor will defend the title against future claims
opts.B: The property is free of undisclosed encumbrances
opts.C: The grantee will have quiet enjoyment of the property
opts.D: The grantor actually owns and has the right to convey the property

questions.exp: The covenant of seisin (or seizin) guarantees that the grantor actually owns and possesses the title they are claiming to convey. It is the first of the six covenants in a general warranty deed.

questions.q: Which type of deed is MOST commonly used in arm's-length real estate sales in Pennsylvania?

opts.A: Quitclaim deed
opts.B: General warranty deed
opts.C: Sheriff's deed
opts.D: Executor's deed

questions.exp: General warranty deeds are the standard deed used in residential real estate sales in Pennsylvania and most other states because they offer the grantee the greatest protection through full covenants covering the entire chain of title.

questions.q: A sheriff's deed is used to transfer title following a:

opts.A: Court-ordered foreclosure sale
opts.B: Gift from parent to child
opts.C: Voluntary sale between private parties
opts.D: Transfer from a decedent's estate

questions.exp: A sheriff's deed is issued by the sheriff following a court-ordered foreclosure or execution sale. It carries no warranty from the grantor (the sheriff) — it is a deed by operation of law.

questions.q: The consideration in a deed need not be the actual purchase price, but must be:

opts.A: At least $1,000
opts.B: Equal to the appraised value
opts.C: Paid in cash only
opts.D: Legally sufficient (even nominal, such as "love and affection")

questions.exp: Consideration in a deed can be nominal — "one dollar and other good and valuable consideration" or "love and affection" (for gifts) is legally sufficient. The deed does not need to state the full purchase price.

questions.q: If a grantor conveys property to a grantee but retains a life estate, which statement is TRUE?

opts.A: The grantor retains the right to use and occupy the property for life
opts.B: The grantee has a leasehold interest only
opts.C: The grantee immediately has full, unrestricted ownership
opts.D: The grantee takes title subject to a mortgage

questions.exp: When the grantor reserves a life estate, the grantor retains the right to possess and use the property for their lifetime. The grantee holds a remainder interest that becomes possessory only upon the grantor's death.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST defines "chain of title"?

opts.A: The successive transfers of ownership from the original grant to the present owner
opts.B: The list of all liens on a property
opts.C: The physical boundaries of a parcel
opts.D: The recorded easements affecting the property

questions.exp: The chain of title is the chronological sequence of recorded documents showing how ownership has passed from one person to the next. A break or defect in the chain creates a cloud on title.

questions.q: Eminent domain differs from adverse possession in that eminent domain:

opts.A: Requires 21 years of possession
opts.B: Requires hostile, open, and notorious use
opts.C: Can only be exercised by private parties
opts.D: Requires payment of just compensation to the property owner

questions.exp: Eminent domain is the government's power to take private property for public use — but it always requires payment of just (fair market value) compensation. Adverse possession requires no compensation but requires long-term hostile possession by a private party.

questions.q: The PRIMARY purpose of recording a deed is to:

opts.A: Make the deed legally valid between buyer and seller
opts.B: Pay the state transfer tax
opts.C: Give constructive notice to the world of the grantee's ownership
opts.D: Obtain a title insurance policy

questions.exp: Recording a deed in the county recorder's office gives constructive notice to all subsequent buyers and creditors. Without recording, a later bona fide purchaser with no actual notice could prevail over the unrecorded deed holder.

questions.q: An abstract of title is BEST described as:

opts.A: A guarantee that the title is free of defects
opts.B: An insurance policy covering title defects
opts.C: A summary of all recorded documents affecting a parcel of land
opts.D: A government certificate of ownership

questions.exp: An abstract of title is a condensed history — a summary — of all recorded instruments (deeds, mortgages, liens, easements, etc.) affecting the property. An attorney reviews it to give a title opinion. It is not a guarantee or insurance policy.

questions.q: A title insurance policy that protects the lender's interest in the property is called a:

opts.A: Owner's (fee) policy
opts.B: Extended coverage policy
opts.C: Binder policy
opts.D: Loan (mortgagee) policy

questions.exp: A loan policy (also called a mortgagee's policy) insures the lender up to the outstanding loan balance. An owner's (fee) policy insures the owner up to the purchase price. Both are issued by title insurance companies.

questions.q: Which of the following would MOST LIKELY appear in a title search but NOT be insured by a standard title insurance policy?

opts.A: Forged deed in the chain of title
opts.B: Undisclosed heir claiming ownership
opts.C: Impersonation of the true owner
opts.D: Encroachments discoverable by an accurate survey

questions.exp: Standard title insurance typically excludes defects that an accurate survey would disclose (e.g., encroachments, boundary disputes). Forgery, undisclosed heirs, and impersonation are generally covered. Extended coverage policies may cover survey matters.

questions.q: Under Pennsylvania's recording act (race-notice statute), a subsequent bona fide purchaser wins over a prior unrecorded deed if the purchaser:

opts.A: Paid the highest price
opts.B: Recorded first regardless of notice
opts.C: Is a licensed real estate agent
opts.D: Had no notice of the prior deed AND recorded first
