questions.exp: Pennsylvania uses a race-notice recording act. To be protected, a subsequent purchaser must (1) pay value, (2) have no actual or constructive notice of prior claims, AND (3) record before the prior claimant.

questions.q: Constructive notice means:

opts.A: The buyer was directly told about a title defect
opts.B: The seller concealed a defect from the buyer
opts.C: Notice that the law presumes everyone has because the information is publicly recorded
opts.D: Notice given in writing by certified mail

questions.exp: Constructive notice is legal knowledge imputed to all parties because the information is recorded in the public records. A buyer is deemed to know about all recorded documents even if they did not personally search them.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of actual notice?

opts.A: A deed recorded in the county recorder's office
opts.B: A lis pendens in the public records
opts.C: The buyer's agent tells the buyer that a neighbor claims an easement
opts.D: The property tax records show a delinquency

questions.exp: Actual notice is direct, firsthand knowledge — information a party personally knows. Being told verbally or in writing about a claim constitutes actual notice. Recorded documents create constructive notice, not actual notice.

questions.q: A lis pendens is recorded to give notice that:

opts.A: The property has been sold
opts.B: A lawsuit is pending that may affect title to the property
opts.C: A mortgage has been paid off
opts.D: The property is being rezoned

questions.exp: A lis pendens ("suit pending") is a recorded notice that there is active litigation affecting the property. Anyone who purchases the property after recording takes it subject to the outcome of that lawsuit.

questions.q: Title insurance differs from other types of insurance in that it:

opts.A: Protects against past events (defects in the chain of title) with a one-time premium
opts.B: Does not cover pre-existing conditions
opts.C: Requires annual premium payments
opts.D: Is required by law in every real estate transaction

questions.exp: Title insurance is unique: it protects against past defects (forgeries, undisclosed heirs, errors in the public record) with a single, one-time premium. Other insurance types (homeowners, auto, life) protect against future events and require ongoing premiums.

questions.q: A Torrens system is a method of title assurance that:

opts.A: Replaces the need for any deed
opts.B: Provides a government certificate of title as conclusive evidence of ownership
opts.C: Insures title through private companies
opts.D: Requires an attorney's title opinion

questions.exp: The Torrens system (used in a few states) involves a court proceeding that results in a government-issued certificate of title. The certificate is conclusive evidence of ownership. Pennsylvania uses a recording system, not the Torrens system.

questions.q: When does a buyer receive constructive notice of a prior recorded easement?

opts.A: Only when the seller discloses it on the disclosure form
opts.B: When the buyer's attorney completes a title search
opts.C: Only if the easement is visible on the property
opts.D: At the moment the easement was recorded, regardless of the buyer's actual knowledge

questions.exp: Constructive notice dates from the time of recording. A buyer is presumed to know about any easement properly recorded in the public records — even if the buyer never personally searched those records.

questions.q: Title evidence MOST commonly used in Pennsylvania residential transactions is:

opts.A: A Torrens certificate
opts.B: Title insurance (owner's and lender's policies)
opts.C: An attorney's abstract and title opinion only
opts.D: A government warranty certificate

questions.exp: In Pennsylvania and most U.S. states, title insurance is the predominant form of title assurance in residential transactions. Lenders almost universally require a loan policy, and buyers are strongly advised to purchase an owner's policy as well.

questions.q: A title search is conducted by examining records at the:

opts.A: State Real Estate Commission
opts.B: Federal land office
opts.C: County recorder of deeds and courthouse
opts.D: Local zoning board

questions.exp: Title searches are conducted at the county recorder of deeds (for deeds, mortgages, liens, easements) and other courthouse offices (for judgments, tax liens, pending lawsuits) where all public land records are maintained.

questions.q: Which of the following would be considered a "cloud on title"?

opts.A: A properly discharged mortgage
opts.B: A recorded easement with a clear legal description
opts.C: A current, recorded deed conveying title to the present owner
opts.D: An unresolved mechanic's lien from a prior owner

questions.exp: A cloud on title is any document or claim that appears to affect ownership or creates doubt about the title's validity. An unresolved lien (even from a prior owner), an old mortgage never formally discharged, or an ambiguous deed can all create a cloud.

questions.q: A title commitment (binder) issued before closing:

opts.A: Is the title company's promise to insure title once stated conditions are met
opts.B: Is a substitute for title insurance
opts.C: Guarantees that the title is perfect
opts.D: Replaces the need for a deed

questions.exp: A title commitment (binder) is issued after the title search and lists the conditions that must be met before the title company will issue the actual insurance policy. It shows what exceptions and requirements apply.

questions.q: If a property has an undisclosed encroachment from a neighbor's fence, a standard (ALTA) title policy:

opts.A: May not cover it unless extended or survey coverage is added
opts.B: Covers it if it was discovered during the title search
opts.C: Automatically covers the loss
opts.D: Covers it because all physical defects are insured

questions.exp: Standard title insurance policies exclude survey matters — including encroachments — that an accurate survey would have disclosed. An ALTA extended coverage policy (with survey) is needed to insure against such physical title risks.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes "marketable title"?

opts.A: Title that is free of all encumbrances
opts.B: Title that a reasonable buyer would accept without fear of litigation
opts.C: Title insured by a nationally recognized company
opts.D: Title that has been examined by a licensed attorney

questions.exp: Marketable title is not necessarily perfect title — it may have minor encumbrances such as easements or covenants. But it must be free of serious defects that would expose the buyer to litigation, and a reasonable, prudent buyer would willingly accept it.

questions.q: If a property owner pays off a mortgage in full, the lender should provide a:

opts.A: New deed to the property
opts.B: Satisfaction of mortgage (mortgage discharge)
opts.C: Reconveyance deed to itself
opts.D: Updated title insurance policy

questions.exp: When a mortgage is paid in full, the lender executes a satisfaction of mortgage (also called a mortgage discharge or release) that should be recorded to remove the mortgage lien from the public record and clear the title.

questions.q: Which type of property records gives notice of a deceased owner's will or estate proceedings affecting title?

opts.A: Orphans' Court or probate records
opts.B: Tax assessment records
opts.C: Recorder of deeds
opts.D: Planning commission files

questions.exp: Wills and estate matters (including letters testamentary, administration of estates) are handled by the Orphans' Court in Pennsylvania. A title searcher must check these records to confirm that title passed properly from a deceased owner.

questions.q: An owner's title insurance policy protects the insured against covered title defects that existed:

opts.A: Before or on the policy date (at the time of closing)
opts.B: Only during the policy period (annual renewal required)
opts.C: After the policy date
opts.D: Only during the insured's lifetime

questions.exp: Title insurance covers defects that existed as of the policy date (the date of closing). It does not cover defects created after issuance. An owner's policy typically remains in force as long as the insured or their heirs have an interest in the property.

questions.q: Which of the following is a required element for a real estate contract to be legally enforceable?

opts.A: Witnessed signatures
opts.B: Mutual consent (offer and acceptance)
opts.C: Notarization
opts.D: Approval by the state real estate commission

questions.exp: A valid contract requires mutual consent (offer and acceptance — "meeting of the minds"), consideration, legal capacity of the parties, and a lawful purpose. For real estate, the Statute of Frauds also requires the agreement to be in writing and signed.

questions.q: The Statute of Frauds requires that contracts for the sale of real estate be:

opts.A: Approved by a licensed attorney
opts.B: Filed with the county recorder
opts.C: In writing and signed by the party to be charged
opts.D: Witnessed by two disinterested parties

questions.exp: The Statute of Frauds (adopted in all states) requires that contracts for the sale of real property, leases over one year, and listing agreements be in writing and signed to be enforceable. Oral real estate sales contracts are generally not enforceable.

questions.q: A contract is VOID when:

opts.A: One party was a minor when signing
opts.B: The contract's purpose is illegal
opts.C: One party was intoxicated when signing
opts.D: One party signed under duress

questions.exp: A void contract has no legal effect from the start — it is treated as if it never existed. A contract for an illegal purpose (e.g., sale of drugs, violation of law) is void. Contracts involving minors, intoxication, or duress are voidable (not void) — they can be disaffirmed by the injured party.

questions.q: An option contract in real estate gives the optionee (buyer) the:

opts.A: Obligation to purchase the property
opts.B: Right to list the property for sale
opts.C: Right, but not the obligation, to purchase the property at a set price within a set time
opts.D: Ownership of the property during the option period

questions.exp: An option contract binds only the seller (optionor) to sell at the agreed price if the buyer chooses to exercise the option. The buyer (optionee) has a right but no obligation to purchase. If the buyer lets the option expire, the seller keeps the option consideration.

questions.q: If a seller accepts a buyer's offer and then mails the acceptance, at what point is the contract formed?

opts.A: When the seller deposits the signed acceptance in the mail (mailbox rule)
opts.B: When the seller signs the acceptance
opts.C: When the buyer receives the signed acceptance
opts.D: When both parties initial the final page

questions.exp: Under the mailbox rule (deposited acceptance rule), a contract is formed when the acceptance is properly placed in the mail — even before the offeror receives it — as long as the offeror authorized mail as a means of acceptance. Many modern PA contracts modify this by specifying delivery or written notice.

questions.q: Earnest money (deposit) in a real estate contract:

opts.A: Is held in escrow to show the buyer's good faith and is applied to the purchase price at closing
opts.B: Becomes the seller's property at contract signing
opts.C: Is always the minimum required by law
opts.D: Is paid directly to the listing broker as their commission

questions.exp: Earnest money demonstrates the buyer's good faith intent to purchase. It is held in escrow (usually by the broker or title company) until closing, where it is credited toward the buyer's purchase price. It does not belong to the seller unless the buyer defaults.

questions.q: A contingency clause in a sales contract allows:

opts.A: Either party to withdraw for any reason at any time
opts.B: A party to exit the contract if a specified condition is not met
opts.C: The seller to increase the price after contract execution
opts.D: The broker to negotiate the terms on behalf of both parties

questions.exp: A contingency (or condition) clause makes the contract's obligations dependent on a specified event occurring (e.g., buyer securing financing, property passing inspection). If the condition is not met, the contingent party may cancel the contract without penalty.

questions.q: Which remedy allows a wronged party in a real estate contract to demand that the other party perform exactly as agreed?

opts.A: Rescission
opts.B: Compensatory damages
opts.C: Liquidated damages
opts.D: Specific performance

questions.exp: Specific performance is a court order requiring a party to perform as agreed. It is commonly sought by buyers when a seller refuses to complete a sale of unique property (real estate) — since money damages may not adequately compensate for the loss of a specific parcel.

questions.q: Liquidated damages in a real estate contract typically means:

opts.A: The buyer gets a cash refund of their earnest money plus interest
opts.B: The court awards damages based on the actual loss
opts.C: The seller must pay twice the earnest money if the seller defaults
opts.D: The parties agree in advance that the earnest money is the seller's sole remedy if the buyer defaults

questions.exp: A liquidated damages clause establishes the amount of damages in advance. In many residential contracts, if the buyer defaults, the seller retains the earnest money as liquidated damages — in full satisfaction of the seller's claim — without further lawsuit.

questions.q: A counteroffer made by the seller in response to a buyer's offer:

opts.A: Keeps the buyer's original offer alive
opts.B: Creates a binding contract immediately
opts.C: Terminates the buyer's original offer and creates a new offer from the seller
opts.D: Must be accepted within 24 hours

questions.exp: A counteroffer is a rejection of the original offer combined with a new offer from the other party. Once a counteroffer is made, the original offer is terminated and the original offeror (buyer) is under no obligation to accept the counteroffer.

questions.q: A contract entered into because one party was threatened with bodily harm is:

opts.A: Void from the start
opts.B: Fully enforceable
opts.C: Valid because the party did sign it
opts.D: Voidable by the party who was threatened

questions.exp: A contract signed under duress (threat of harm) is voidable — the coerced party may disaffirm it. It is not void because it has the appearance of consent, but the consent was not truly free. The wronged party can choose to enforce or rescind the contract.

questions.q: A bilateral contract is one in which:

opts.A: Only one party makes a promise
opts.B: Payment is deferred to a later date
opts.C: A third party guarantees performance
opts.D: Both parties exchange promises

questions.exp: In a bilateral contract, both parties exchange binding promises (e.g., "I promise to sell; you promise to buy"). A typical real estate sales contract is bilateral. An option contract, where only the seller is bound, is a unilateral contract.

questions.q: When a buyer fails to complete a purchase without legal cause, the seller may:

opts.A: Automatically keep all earnest money and the property
opts.B: Retain earnest money (if so agreed), sue for damages, or seek specific performance
opts.C: Only sue for specific performance
opts.D: Relist the property only after returning the earnest money

questions.exp: When a buyer defaults, the seller has several potential remedies depending on the contract language: (1) retain the earnest money as liquidated damages, (2) sue for actual damages, or (3) seek specific performance in court. The seller typically chooses the most advantageous remedy.

questions.q: An executed contract is one in which:

opts.A: Only the offer has been signed
opts.B: The parties are still performing their obligations
opts.C: All parties have fully performed their obligations
opts.D: The contract was signed before witnesses

questions.exp: An executed contract is fully performed by all parties. At closing, when the deed is delivered and the purchase price paid, the sales contract becomes fully executed. Before closing, when obligations are still pending, it is an executory contract.

questions.q: Which of the following would make a contract voidable (not void)?

opts.A: The contract requires an illegal act
opts.B: One party lacked contractual capacity due to age (minor)
opts.C: There was never a meeting of the minds
opts.D: No consideration was exchanged by either party

questions.exp: A contract with a minor is voidable — the minor may disaffirm (cancel) it, but the adult party is bound unless the minor cancels. A contract with an illegal purpose is void; a contract with no consideration lacks a required element and is unenforceable.

questions.q: An "as-is" clause in a real estate contract means the seller:

opts.A: Need not disclose any defects even if known
opts.B: Is exempt from all Pennsylvania disclosure laws
opts.C: Will not make repairs, but must still disclose known material defects
opts.D: Reduces the sale price by the cost of all repairs

questions.exp: An "as-is" clause means the seller will not make repairs and the buyer accepts the property in its current condition. However, it does NOT relieve the seller of the duty to disclose known material defects under Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law.

questions.q: Novation in contract law means:

opts.A: Replacing an existing contract with a new one, releasing the original party from liability
opts.B: One party assigns their rights to a third party
opts.C: Adding a new contingency to an existing contract
opts.D: Extending the closing date by written amendment

questions.exp: Novation substitutes a new party or a new obligation for an old one, with the consent of all parties, and releases the original party from liability. For example, if a seller's mortgage is novated, the buyer takes over the loan and the seller is released from any obligation on it.

questions.q: A real estate licensee may prepare which of the following contract documents in Pennsylvania?

opts.A: Custom legal instruments drafted from scratch
opts.B: Legal opinions on title matters
opts.C: Title insurance commitments
opts.D: Standard pre-printed contract forms approved for use

questions.exp: Pennsylvania licensees may fill in pre-printed standardized contract forms (e.g., the PAR Standard Agreement) without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law. They may NOT draft custom legal instruments, give legal opinions, or prepare title commitments.

questions.q: A contract that is "implied in fact" is created by:

opts.A: The conduct and actions of the parties
opts.B: Oral agreement followed by a handshake
opts.C: Written agreement signed by all parties
opts.D: Court order

questions.exp: An implied-in-fact contract arises from the behavior and conduct of the parties rather than express words (written or oral). For example, regularly hiring a contractor and paying them creates an implied contract for future work at the same rate.

questions.q: Which of the following terminates an offer BEFORE acceptance?

opts.A: The death of the offeror
opts.B: The offeree requests more time to decide
opts.C: The offeree reads the offer carefully
opts.D: The offeree shares the offer with an attorney

questions.exp: An offer terminates automatically upon the death or incapacity of either party before acceptance, expiration of the time stated, rejection, counteroffer, revocation by the offeror (before acceptance), or by operation of law.

questions.q: In a mortgage loan, the borrower is called the:

opts.A: Mortgagee
opts.B: Beneficiary
opts.C: Trustee
opts.D: Mortgagor

questions.exp: The mortgagor is the borrower who pledges (mortgages) the property as security for the loan. The mortgagee is the lender who receives the mortgage. Memory tip: the mortgagor "gives" the mortgage to get the loan.

questions.q: The promissory note in a real estate loan transaction is:

opts.A: The security instrument pledging the property
opts.B: The lien recorded against the property
opts.C: The borrower's personal promise to repay the debt
opts.D: The title insurance commitment

questions.exp: The promissory note is the borrower's personal promise (IOU) to repay the loan under stated terms. The mortgage (or deed of trust) is the separate security instrument that creates the lien on the property. Both documents are signed at closing.

questions.q: In a fully amortized mortgage, monthly payments are structured so that:

opts.A: Early payments are mostly principal with interest added later
opts.B: The payment amount decreases each month as principal is paid
opts.C: The loan balance reaches zero at the end of the term
opts.D: A balloon payment is required at the end

questions.exp: Full amortization means each equal payment includes both principal and interest, and the loan is completely paid off by the last scheduled payment. Early payments are mostly interest; later payments are mostly principal — but the balance always reaches zero on schedule.

questions.q: A balloon mortgage requires:

opts.A: Monthly payments that are higher than a fully amortized loan
opts.B: No monthly payments until the end
opts.C: A large lump-sum payment due at the end of a short loan term
opts.D: Annual principal payments only

questions.exp: A balloon mortgage has relatively low monthly payments (often interest-only or partially amortized) with a large final "balloon" payment of the remaining principal balance due at the end of the loan term (e.g., 5 or 7 years).

questions.q: The loan-to-value (LTV) ratio is calculated as:

opts.A: Loan amount ÷ appraised value (or purchase price, whichever is lower)
opts.B: Property value ÷ loan amount
opts.C: Loan amount ÷ borrower's income
opts.D: Monthly payment ÷ gross income

questions.exp: LTV = Loan amount ÷ property value (the lower of appraised value or purchase price). A higher LTV indicates more lender risk. Conventional loans above 80% LTV typically require private mortgage insurance (PMI).

questions.q: Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) is required on conventional loans when the LTV exceeds:
questions.exp: Conventional lenders require PMI when the LTV exceeds 80% (i.e., the down payment is less than 20%). PMI protects the lender — not the borrower — against loss if the borrower defaults. Under the Homeowners Protection Act, PMI must be cancelled when LTV reaches 78%.

questions.q: A buyer pays 2 discount points to obtain a mortgage. One point equals:

opts.A: 1% of the property purchase price
opts.B: 1% of the loan amount
opts.C: $100 regardless of loan size
opts.D: 0.5% of the loan amount

questions.exp: One discount point = 1% of the loan amount, paid at closing to "buy down" (reduce) the interest rate. Two points on a $200,000 loan = $4,000 paid to the lender. Each point typically lowers the rate by about ⅛% (0.125%).

questions.q: An adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) differs from a fixed-rate mortgage in that:

opts.A: An ARM's interest rate can change periodically based on an index
opts.B: An ARM always has a lower interest rate for the life of the loan
opts.C: The monthly payment is always fixed on an ARM
opts.D: ARMs cannot be used for residential properties

questions.exp: An ARM has an interest rate that adjusts periodically (annually, semi-annually, etc.) based on a benchmark index (e.g., SOFR) plus a margin. ARMs typically offer a lower initial rate than fixed-rate loans but carry the risk of rate increases over time.

questions.q: Which clause in a mortgage gives the lender the right to demand full payment of the loan balance if the property is sold?

opts.A: Due-on-sale (alienation) clause
opts.B: Acceleration clause
opts.C: Prepayment penalty clause
opts.D: Subordination clause

questions.exp: A due-on-sale (alienation) clause prevents the buyer from assuming the seller's mortgage without the lender's consent. If the property is sold, the lender may demand full repayment of the outstanding balance. This prevents assumption of below-market-rate loans.

questions.q: An acceleration clause allows the lender to:

opts.A: Increase the interest rate during the loan term
opts.B: Reduce the required monthly payment
opts.C: Transfer the mortgage to a different lender
opts.D: Demand the entire loan balance due immediately upon default

questions.exp: An acceleration clause ("call clause") in the promissory note or mortgage lets the lender declare the entire unpaid loan balance immediately due and payable upon the borrower's default. Without it, the lender could only sue for each missed payment individually.

questions.q: A FHA-insured loan requires a mortgage insurance premium (MIP). This insurance protects:

opts.A: The borrower against job loss
opts.B: The FHA/lender against borrower default
opts.C: The property against damage
opts.D: The title company against prior liens

questions.exp: FHA mortgage insurance (MIP) protects the lender and the FHA insurance fund if the borrower defaults. Because the government insures the loan, FHA can accept lower down payments (as low as 3.5%) and is more accessible to first-time buyers. MIP does NOT protect the borrower.

questions.q: A VA-guaranteed loan is available to eligible veterans and:

opts.A: May require no down payment and has no PMI
opts.B: Always requires private mortgage insurance
opts.C: Requires a minimum 10% down payment
opts.D: Is limited to rural properties

questions.exp: VA loans are guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Eligible veterans, service members, and surviving spouses can finance up to 100% of the purchase price with no down payment. There is no monthly PMI, though a one-time funding fee is required (unless exempt).

questions.q: Predatory lending practices are characterized by:

opts.A: Low interest rates and transparent fees
opts.B: Requiring large down payments
opts.C: Requiring borrowers to use a specific real estate agent
opts.D: Excessive fees, deceptive terms, or targeting vulnerable borrowers

questions.exp: Predatory lending involves abusive or deceptive practices — such as charging excessive fees, misrepresenting loan terms, equity stripping, loan flipping, or targeting elderly or minority borrowers with unsuitable products. RESPA, TILA, and the Dodd-Frank Act address these practices.

questions.q: The Truth-in-Lending Act (TILA) requires lenders to disclose the:

opts.A: Lender's credit score requirements
opts.B: Property's appraised value
opts.C: Lender's profit margin on the loan
opts.D: Annual Percentage Rate (APR) and total financing costs

questions.exp: TILA (Regulation Z) requires lenders to clearly disclose the APR (total cost of borrowing, expressed annually), the total finance charge, the amount financed, and the total of all payments — so borrowers can compare loan offers on equal footing.

questions.q: Redlining is the illegal practice of:

opts.A: Marking property boundaries with red lines on plats
opts.B: Refusing to make loans or restricting credit in certain geographic areas based on race or national origin
opts.C: Overcharging for title insurance in certain areas
opts.D: Setting interest rates above the legal maximum

questions.exp: Redlining is the discriminatory practice of denying or limiting financial services (loans, insurance) in certain neighborhoods based on the racial or ethnic composition of the area. It violates the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act.

questions.q: The secondary mortgage market is best described as:

opts.A: A market for second mortgages only
opts.B: The market where existing mortgages are bought and sold among investors
opts.C: A market where borrowers get their second loan
opts.D: A market for commercial mortgages only

questions.exp: The secondary mortgage market is where originators sell mortgage loans to investors (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, Ginnie Mae, private investors). This replenishes the lenders' funds so they can make new loans, keeping the primary mortgage market liquid.

questions.q: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are known as:

opts.A: Federal regulatory agencies
opts.B: Insurance funds for FHA and VA loans
opts.C: Government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) that support the secondary mortgage market
opts.D: Federal lenders that originate mortgages directly

questions.exp: Fannie Mae (FNMA) and Freddie Mac (FHLMC) are GSEs that purchase conforming mortgages from lenders, package them into mortgage-backed securities, and sell them to investors. They do not originate loans directly.

questions.q: A purchase money mortgage (PMM) is:

opts.A: A mortgage used exclusively for purchasing investment property
opts.B: Seller financing — the seller accepts a mortgage from the buyer as part of the purchase price
opts.C: A loan from a bank to buy the property
opts.D: A bridge loan from the buyer's current property

questions.exp: A purchase money mortgage occurs when the seller accepts a mortgage from the buyer (instead of or in addition to the cash price). The seller essentially lends the buyer money to complete the purchase. It is a common form of seller financing.

questions.q: Which type of lien automatically has FIRST priority over all other liens on a property?

opts.A: First mortgage recorded
opts.B: Judgment lien
opts.C: Real property tax lien
opts.D: Mechanic's lien

questions.exp: Real property tax liens are granted "super priority" — they are senior to all other liens regardless of recording date. Even a first mortgage recorded decades before a tax lien is subordinate to the tax lien. This priority ensures local governments collect taxes.

questions.q: A wrap-around mortgage (all-inclusive deed of trust) involves:

opts.A: The lender providing two separate loans simultaneously
opts.B: A second lien that is subordinate only in default situations
opts.C: A borrower refinancing to combine two existing loans
opts.D: A new mortgage that includes (wraps around) an existing underlying mortgage

questions.exp: In a wrap-around mortgage, the seller finances the buyer with a new (larger) mortgage that includes the outstanding balance of an existing underlying loan. The buyer makes one payment to the seller, who then makes payments on the underlying mortgage. This is a form of creative seller financing.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Real Estate License and Registration Act (RELRA) is administered by:

opts.A: The Pennsylvania Department of State, Bureau of Licensing
opts.B: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
opts.C: The National Association of REALTORS®
opts.D: The Pennsylvania Department of Banking

questions.exp: RELRA grants authority to the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission (PREC) to administer, regulate, and enforce the real estate licensing laws. The Commission has the power to issue, suspend, and revoke licenses.

questions.q: Under Pennsylvania law, which of the following activities requires a real estate license?

opts.A: A person negotiating the sale of real estate on behalf of another for compensation
opts.B: An attorney handling a client's real estate matter as an incidental part of law practice
opts.C: An owner selling their own home
opts.D: A property manager who manages only one property for a single owner

questions.exp: A license is required to act on behalf of another person in real estate transactions — including negotiating sales, exchanges, leases, or rentals — for compensation. Exemptions include property owners selling their own property and attorneys acting incidentally in their legal practice.

questions.q: A salesperson's license in Pennsylvania must be held by:

opts.A: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
opts.B: The salesperson themselves, independent of any broker
opts.C: A licensed real estate broker
opts.D: The county association of REALTORS®

questions.exp: A salesperson's license in Pennsylvania must be held by (affiliated with) a licensed broker. Salespersons may not operate independently — all their real estate activities must be conducted under their employing broker's supervision.

questions.q: Pennsylvania continuing education for license renewal requires licensees to complete how many hours per renewal cycle?

opts.A: 7 hours
opts.B: 10 hours
opts.C: 14 hours
opts.D: 20 hours

questions.exp: Pennsylvania requires 14 hours of continuing education (CE) every two-year renewal cycle. The mandatory core module covers topics designated by the Commission, and the remaining hours may be elective real estate topics.

questions.q: Which of the following is grounds for license suspension or revocation under Pennsylvania law?

opts.A: Failure to attend a REALTOR® convention
opts.B: Selling a property below market value
opts.C: Representing more than three clients simultaneously
opts.D: Commingling client funds with personal funds

questions.exp: Commingling — mixing client (escrow) funds with a licensee's personal or operating funds — is a serious violation under RELRA and can result in license suspension or revocation. Escrow funds must be kept in a separate, designated account.

questions.q: A real estate broker who operates under a fictitious name (trade name) must:

opts.A: Register the name with the National Association of REALTORS®
opts.B: Get approval from the local zoning board
opts.C: Register the trade name with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
opts.D: Use only the broker's legal name in all advertising

questions.exp: Any fictitious or trade name used by a broker must be registered with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission. The registered name must appear in all advertising. This prevents deceptive or misleading business names.

questions.q: Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law requires the seller to disclose:

opts.A: The seller's motivation for selling
opts.B: Known material defects that affect the value or habitability of the property
opts.C: The seller's mortgage payoff amount
opts.D: Whether any previous offers were made on the property

questions.exp: The PA Seller Disclosure Law (Act 78) requires sellers of residential property to provide buyers with a written disclosure of known material defects — conditions that affect the property's value, habitability, or safety. Non-disclosure of known defects can expose the seller (and agent) to liability.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, an associate broker differs from a salesperson in that the associate broker:

opts.A: Earns a higher commission by law
opts.B: Does not need to be affiliated with a broker
opts.C: Has met the experience and education requirements to be a broker but chooses to work under another broker
opts.D: Can supervise other associate brokers

questions.exp: An associate broker in Pennsylvania has fulfilled all the requirements for a broker's license (education and experience) but works under another (employing) broker rather than independently. The associate broker has broker-level qualifications but broker-level independence only if they obtain their own broker license.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Real Estate Recovery Fund exists to:

opts.A: Pay for continuing education of licensees
opts.B: Fund the operation of the Real Estate Commission
opts.C: Reimburse brokers for uncollected commissions
opts.D: Compensate victims of licensee fraud or misrepresentation who cannot collect a judgment

questions.exp: The Real Estate Recovery Fund (funded by license fees) compensates consumers who suffer financial harm from a licensee's fraud, misrepresentation, or deceit and are unable to collect a court judgment from the licensee. Payment from the fund results in automatic license suspension until repaid.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about earnest money handling in Pennsylvania?

opts.A: Brokers may hold earnest money in their personal accounts for convenience
opts.B: Earnest money must always be deposited within 24 hours of receipt
opts.C: Only the seller's attorney may hold earnest money
opts.D: Earnest money must be deposited in a separate escrow account and not commingled with the broker's funds

questions.exp: Pennsylvania law requires that all funds received by a broker in a fiduciary capacity (earnest money, deposits) be placed in a separate escrow (trust) account. These funds must NEVER be commingled with the broker's personal or business funds.

questions.q: An individual whose license has lapsed may NOT:

opts.A: Study for the licensing exam
opts.B: Attend real estate education classes
opts.C: Renew their license at a higher fee
opts.D: Perform any real estate brokerage activities

questions.exp: A licensee with a lapsed license has no authority to perform any real estate activities (negotiate, show, list, etc.) until the license is properly renewed. Practicing on a lapsed license is the equivalent of practicing without a license.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, a licensed broker who wants to open their own real estate firm must:

opts.A: First obtain a salesperson's license
opts.B: Register the firm with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
opts.C: Form a partnership with another broker
opts.D: File a business plan with the Department of Banking

questions.exp: A broker who opens a real estate office (brokerage firm) must register the firm's name with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission. Each office must have a designated broker of record responsible for the office's operations.

questions.q: Which of the following individuals is exempt from the Pennsylvania real estate license requirement?

opts.A: An attorney-in-fact (power of attorney) acting for a single principal
opts.B: A business that lists and rents vacation properties for owners
opts.C: A person who negotiates leases for multiple landlords for a fee
opts.D: A buyer's agent working on a flat-fee basis

questions.exp: An attorney-in-fact acting under a power of attorney for a single principal (not for compensation from third parties) is exempt from the license requirement. The exemption requires that the person not be in the general business of real estate for others.

questions.q: A Pennsylvania real estate salesperson may receive compensation:

opts.A: Directly from the buyer or seller as the transaction is completed
opts.B: From any party involved in the transaction
opts.C: From any licensed broker in the state
opts.D: Only through the employing broker

questions.exp: Under RELRA, a salesperson or associate broker may receive compensation only through their employing broker. Direct payment from clients, customers, or other parties to the salesperson (bypassing the broker) is prohibited.

questions.q: The Consumer Notice in Pennsylvania is required to be provided to:

opts.A: Only buyers who are first-time homeowners
opts.B: Consumers at the first substantive contact with a licensee
opts.C: Sellers at the time of listing only
opts.D: Only parties who hire the agent as a buyer's agent

questions.exp: The Pennsylvania Consumer Notice (agency disclosure) must be provided at the first substantive contact with a consumer — whether buyer or seller. It explains the types of agency relationships available and which relationship the licensee is proposing.

questions.q: Blockbusting (panic selling) is:

opts.A: Legal if all parties consent to the technique
opts.B: Illegal — inducing owners to sell by suggesting that minority groups are moving into the neighborhood
opts.C: Permitted as long as the agent discloses the practice
opts.D: Only illegal in federally funded housing

questions.exp: Blockbusting is the illegal practice of inducing homeowners to sell (often at below-market prices) by making representations that members of a protected class are entering the neighborhood. It violates the federal Fair Housing Act and Pennsylvania law.

questions.q: Pennsylvania law requires that real estate licensees complete pre-licensing education of:

opts.A: 75 hours for salesperson, 240 hours for broker
opts.B: 60 hours for salesperson, 120 hours for broker
opts.C: 40 hours for salesperson, 80 hours for broker
opts.D: 90 hours for salesperson, 150 hours for broker

questions.exp: Pennsylvania requires 75 clock hours of approved pre-licensing education for salesperson applicants and 240 hours for broker applicants (plus experience requirements). These hours must be completed at a Commission-approved school before taking the state licensing exam.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "net listing" prohibition in Pennsylvania?

opts.A: To protect sellers from agents who might take excess profits above a set price
opts.B: To require all listings to be on the MLS
opts.C: To ensure the seller pays the minimum commission
opts.D: To ensure the buyer pays a fair price

questions.exp: Net listings (where the agent's commission is any amount above a specified net to the seller) are prohibited or heavily restricted in many states, including Pennsylvania, because they create a conflict of interest — the agent profits more by getting the highest price possible at the expense of the seller's interest.

questions.q: When a broker's license is revoked or surrendered, the salespersons affiliated with that broker:

opts.A: Automatically lose their licenses permanently
opts.B: Continue operating independently until they find a new broker
opts.C: Must affiliate with another licensed broker to continue practicing
opts.D: Revert to unlicensed status permanently

questions.exp: When a broker's license is revoked or surrendered, affiliated salespersons cannot operate independently. They must transfer their license to another licensed broker. Their salesperson licenses remain valid during the transition — they simply cannot act until affiliated with a new broker.

questions.q: A licensee who engages in misrepresentation of a material fact during a real estate transaction may face:

opts.A: Both Commission disciplinary action AND civil liability to harmed parties
opts.B: Only a Commission investigation
opts.C: Only a private lawsuit from the harmed party
opts.D: Criminal prosecution only

questions.exp: Misrepresentation of material facts exposes a licensee to multiple consequences: (1) Commission disciplinary action (license suspension/revocation), (2) civil lawsuit for damages by harmed parties, and (3) potentially criminal charges for fraud. These remedies are not mutually exclusive.

questions.q: The term "REALTOR®" refers to:

opts.A: A member of the National Association of REALTORS® who subscribes to its Code of Ethics
opts.B: A licensed broker only
opts.C: Any licensed real estate agent in the United States
opts.D: Any real estate professional who has passed the state exam

questions.exp: REALTOR® is a federally registered trademark of the National Association of REALTORS® (NAR). Only members who subscribe to the NAR Code of Ethics may use the term. Not every licensed agent is a REALTOR®.

questions.q: Multiple Listing Service (MLS) rules generally require that a listing be submitted:

opts.A: Only after the property has been shown at least twice
opts.B: At the time the listing contract is signed
opts.C: Within a set time period after the listing agreement is signed (commonly 24-48 hours)
opts.D: Only once the seller has accepted an offer

questions.exp: MLS participation rules (and NAR Clear Cooperation Policy) require listings to be submitted to the MLS within a specified time period — typically within one to two business days of signing the listing agreement — to ensure broad market exposure and cooperation among members.

questions.q: A real estate broker earns a commission WHEN:

opts.A: The listing agreement is signed
opts.B: The seller accepts a written offer
opts.C: The broker produces a ready, willing, and able buyer on the seller's terms
opts.D: The deed is recorded at closing

questions.exp: Legally, a broker's commission is earned when they produce a "ready, willing, and able" buyer who meets the seller's terms. However, many listing agreements specify that commission is payable only at closing — so the payment obligation may not arise unless the sale closes.

questions.q: An independent contractor real estate salesperson, unlike an employee, typically:

opts.A: Pays their own self-employment taxes and is not provided employee benefits
opts.B: Has taxes withheld by the broker
opts.C: Receives a regular salary
opts.D: Must work set hours determined by the broker

questions.exp: Most salespersons are classified as independent contractors. They receive no salary or employee benefits, no tax withholding, and set their own hours. They must pay their own self-employment taxes (Social Security + Medicare) and generally provide their own equipment.

questions.q: Which type of real estate brokerage firm concentrates on a specific geographic area or property type?

opts.A: Franchise brokerage
opts.B: Virtual brokerage
opts.C: Boutique (specialty) brokerage
opts.D: Referral brokerage

questions.exp: A boutique or specialty brokerage focuses on a niche — a specific neighborhood, luxury market, commercial sector, or property type. This specialization allows deeper market expertise within that segment. Franchises use a brand license model; virtual brokerages have no physical office.

questions.q: E&O (Errors and Omissions) insurance protects a licensee against:

opts.A: Client injuries on a property they showed
opts.B: Property damage at the listed property
opts.C: Claims arising from professional mistakes or omissions during real estate transactions
opts.D: Criminal charges for license law violations

questions.exp: E&O insurance is professional liability insurance that covers real estate licensees against claims of negligence, errors, or omissions made while performing professional services. It does not cover intentional wrongdoing, criminal acts, or physical property damage.

questions.q: A franchise real estate company arrangement means:

opts.A: The franchisee is owned and controlled by the franchisor
opts.B: All commission income flows to the franchisor
opts.C: The franchisee must share all listings with the franchisor
opts.D: The franchisee pays fees to use the franchisor's trade name, systems, and training

questions.exp: In a franchise arrangement, an independently owned brokerage (franchisee) pays royalties and fees to use a national brand's name, advertising, technology, and training programs. The franchisee operates independently but benefits from brand recognition.

questions.q: A "desk fee" arrangement in a real estate office typically means:

opts.A: The broker pays the agent a salary plus a monthly bonus
opts.B: The agent pays the broker a fixed monthly fee and keeps a higher percentage of commissions
opts.C: The agent receives 100% of earned commissions but pays the broker a flat monthly fee for office use
opts.D: The broker charges each agent per transaction regardless of income

questions.exp: A desk fee (or flat-fee) arrangement is a 100% commission model where the agent pays the broker a fixed monthly fee (for office space, support, and access to services) and retains the full commission. It favors high-producing agents who can cover the desk fee with a few transactions.

questions.q: The primary duty of a property manager to the property owner is:

opts.A: Achieving the owner's investment objectives while maintaining the property
opts.B: Maintaining the property's physical condition only
opts.C: Maximizing tenant satisfaction at all costs
opts.D: Keeping all rents below market rate to reduce vacancy

questions.exp: A property manager's primary duty is to the owner: to achieve the owner's investment goals (income, preservation of value, appreciation) while maintaining the physical asset. This may include minimizing vacancy, maintaining rents at market rate, controlling expenses, and overseeing capital improvements.

questions.q: Which business structure offers its owners (members) personal liability protection while avoiding corporate double taxation?

opts.A: Sole proprietorship
opts.B: General partnership
opts.C: C corporation
opts.D: Limited Liability Company (LLC)

questions.exp: An LLC provides members with limited personal liability (like a corporation) while allowing pass-through taxation (like a partnership or sole proprietorship). Income and losses flow to members' personal tax returns, avoiding the double taxation of a C corporation.

questions.q: The National Association of REALTORS® Code of Ethics places the REALTOR®'s duty to the client:

opts.A: Below duties to the public
opts.B: Equal to duties to other REALTORS®
opts.C: Above all other duties with no exceptions
opts.D: First, but also requires obligations to the public and other REALTORS®

questions.exp: The NAR Code of Ethics establishes a hierarchy: duties to clients and customers come first, then duties to the public, then duties to other REALTORS®. However, ethical obligations to the public (such as not deceiving) continue even in client representation.

questions.q: A real estate professional specializing in commercial investment properties would MOST likely hold which designation?

opts.A: ABR (Accredited Buyer's Representative)
opts.B: CCIM (Certified Commercial Investment Member)
opts.C: GRI (Graduate, REALTOR® Institute)
opts.D: CRB (Certified Real Estate Brokerage Manager)

questions.exp: The CCIM designation (Certified Commercial Investment Member) focuses on commercial real estate investment analysis, market analysis, and financial analysis. ABR focuses on buyer representation; GRI is a broad knowledge designation; CRB focuses on brokerage management.

questions.q: Which federal law governs the settlement (closing) procedures for residential real estate transactions?

opts.A: Truth-in-Lending Act (TILA)
opts.B: Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)
opts.C: Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA)
opts.D: Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA)

questions.exp: RESPA (Regulation X) governs the settlement process for federally related mortgage loans. It requires disclosure of settlement costs, prohibits kickbacks and referral fees between settlement service providers, and regulates escrow accounts.

questions.q: Under RESPA, kickbacks for the referral of settlement services are:

opts.A: Permitted if disclosed to the consumer
opts.B: Permitted if split equally between parties
opts.C: Prohibited — they are illegal regardless of disclosure
opts.D: Permitted between licensed real estate agents only

questions.exp: RESPA Section 8 strictly prohibits kickbacks and referral fees for settlement services (title, escrow, appraisal, etc.). The prohibition is absolute — disclosure does not make it legal. Violations can result in criminal prosecution, fines, and civil liability.

questions.q: An Affiliated Business Arrangement (AfBA or RESPA Section 8(c)(4)) allows:

opts.A: Unlimited referral fees between any service providers
opts.B: Referring parties to receive a return on investment from affiliated settlement service companies, with proper disclosure
opts.C: A brokerage to require clients to use its affiliated services
opts.D: Title companies to pay agents for each referral without disclosure

questions.exp: RESPA permits affiliated business arrangements if: (1) the arrangement is disclosed to the consumer in writing, (2) the consumer is not required to use the affiliated service, and (3) the only payment is a return on ownership interest. The consumer retains freedom of choice.

questions.q: A licensee who earns commissions from referrals to other brokers or agents for out-of-area properties is operating as a:

opts.A: Dual agent
opts.B: Referral agent
opts.C: Designated agent
opts.D: Transaction coordinator

questions.exp: A referral agent's primary business is referring clients to other real estate professionals (often in different markets or specialties) in exchange for a referral fee — a portion of the commission earned when the transaction closes. The referral agent does not conduct the actual transaction.

questions.q: Which principle of real estate investment compares a property's income to its value?

opts.A: Gross rent multiplier only
opts.B: Depreciation schedule
opts.C: Loan-to-value ratio
opts.D: Capitalization rate (cap rate)

questions.exp: The capitalization rate (cap rate) = Net Operating Income ÷ Property Value. It expresses the relationship between a property's income and its market value, and is used to estimate value or compare investment properties. A higher cap rate generally indicates higher risk/return.

questions.q: A real estate licensee who manages property for an owner acts as a:

opts.A: Agent (fiduciary) of the property owner
opts.B: Sub-agent of the tenant
opts.C: Trustee
opts.D: Independent principal

questions.exp: A property manager is the owner's agent with fiduciary duties (loyalty, obedience, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, reasonable care) to the owner. When managing property, the licensee must put the owner's interests first.

questions.q: A licensee who provides a buyer with a Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) is:

opts.A: Providing an informal price opinion based on similar sales, to assist with purchase or listing decisions
opts.B: Providing a guaranteed value to the buyer
opts.C: Performing a formal appraisal
opts.D: Violating their license if the property is listed with another agent

questions.exp: A CMA is an informal analysis by a licensee using recent comparable sales data to estimate a property's market value range. It is not a formal appraisal, which must be performed by a licensed/certified appraiser. A CMA assists clients in deciding offer or listing prices.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law (UTPCPL) is relevant to real estate because it:

opts.A: Sets maximum commissions licensees may charge
opts.B: Prohibits deceptive, unfair, or misleading conduct in real estate transactions
opts.C: Regulates the interest rates on real estate loans
opts.D: Requires sellers to warrant all property conditions

questions.exp: The UTPCPL prohibits unfair or deceptive acts and practices in trade and commerce, including real estate. Consumers harmed by such conduct may recover actual damages, attorney's fees, and potentially treble damages. Licensees who misrepresent material facts can be sued under this statute.

questions.q: A cooperating broker who procures a buyer for a property listed by another broker is typically entitled to:

opts.A: The full listing commission
opts.B: A share of the listing commission as agreed in the MLS or cooperation agreement
opts.C: A flat fee from the buyer
opts.D: A separate commission paid by the buyer's lender

questions.exp: When a property is listed in the MLS, the listing broker offers a cooperating commission to buyer's agents. The cooperating (selling) broker typically receives a percentage of the total commission, split according to the MLS offer of compensation or a separate agreement.

questions.q: A salesperson leaves their broker without a new broker. Their license status becomes:

opts.A: Inactive until transferred to or held by a new broker
opts.B: Suspended by the Commission
opts.C: Automatically transferred to the state
opts.D: Revoked by operation of law

questions.exp: When a salesperson is no longer affiliated with a broker, their license becomes inactive. They cannot perform any real estate activities while inactive. To reactivate, they must affiliate with a new licensed broker and complete the transfer with the Commission.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes a "procuring cause" dispute?

opts.A: A seller refuses to pay any commission
opts.B: Two buyers make simultaneous offers
opts.C: Two brokers both claim to have been the agent whose efforts produced the buyer
opts.D: The listing agent and buyer's agent disagree on property value

questions.exp: Procuring cause is the broker/agent who started an uninterrupted chain of events that resulted in the sale. Disputes arise when two agents each claim their efforts were the procuring cause. MLS boards and arbitration panels resolve such disputes.

questions.q: A broker may share commission with an unlicensed person:

opts.A: If the unlicensed person assisted in finding the buyer
opts.B: Never — paying commission to an unlicensed person is prohibited
opts.C: If the unlicensed person is a relative of the broker
opts.D: If the amount is under $500

questions.exp: Pennsylvania (and virtually all states) prohibit paying real estate compensation to an unlicensed person for activities requiring a license. This is a fundamental rule protecting the public. Violating this prohibition subjects the broker's license to disciplinary action.

questions.q: A broker operating as an independent firm (not part of a franchise) is known as a:

opts.A: Corporate broker
opts.B: Referral broker
opts.C: Independent broker
opts.D: Sub-agent broker

questions.exp: An independent broker operates a brokerage under their own name (or a registered trade name) without affiliation with a franchise system. They retain all commissions but also bear all marketing, technology, and operating costs independently.

questions.q: Under the NAR Code of Ethics, REALTORS® must disclose all known facts that materially affect the value of residential real property to:

opts.A: All parties in the transaction
opts.B: The MLS database only
opts.C: The listing broker only
opts.D: Only the party who hired the REALTOR®

questions.exp: NAR Code of Ethics Article 2 requires REALTORS® to avoid misrepresentation and to disclose all known material facts to all parties. This duty extends beyond the client relationship — it is an obligation to the public and to all parties to the transaction.

questions.q: A salesperson who uses the broker's business cards but lists their personal cell phone and private email is:

opts.A: Potentially violating advertising rules if the broker's name is not prominently featured
opts.B: Required to do so under MLS rules
opts.C: Fully compliant if the broker approves
opts.D: Only required to include broker info on the MLS listing

questions.exp: Pennsylvania law requires that all advertising by a licensee clearly identify the employing broker. Personal contact information on business cards or advertising must still include the broker's name and registered trade name so the public knows who the licensee works for.

questions.q: When a buyer's offer is rejected, the broker who submitted the offer must:

opts.A: Immediately find a new buyer
opts.B: Return the earnest money to the broker's account
opts.C: File a written report with the Commission
opts.D: Promptly communicate the rejection to the buyer and return the earnest money

questions.exp: Upon rejection of an offer, the broker/agent must promptly inform the buyer of the rejection and arrange for the return of any earnest money deposited. Failure to do so may breach the agent's fiduciary duty and could expose the broker to liability.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, a real estate firm may be organized as all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: A sole proprietorship
opts.B: A general partnership with both licensed and unlicensed partners sharing profits from brokerage
opts.C: A partnership
opts.D: A corporation

questions.exp: While firms may be sole proprietorships, corporations, or partnerships, a partnership that includes unlicensed persons sharing in brokerage commissions (activities requiring a license) is not permissible. The managing partner must be a licensed broker, and unlicensed persons may not profit from licensed activities.

questions.q: The listing broker presents all offers to the seller. If two offers arrive simultaneously, the broker must:

opts.A: Present only the highest-priced offer
opts.B: Present only the offer most likely to close
opts.C: Present the offers one at a time, starting with the later-received offer
opts.D: Present both offers promptly to the seller

questions.exp: A listing broker has a fiduciary duty to present all offers to the seller promptly. The broker may not screen or prioritize offers based on the broker's preferences — all offers (including simultaneous ones) must be presented so the seller can make an informed decision.

questions.q: A real estate broker who is also the principal buyer in a transaction must:

opts.A: Have the transaction handled by a different broker
opts.B: Refuse to earn any commission
opts.C: Not participate in the transaction in any capacity
opts.D: Disclose their licensed status and financial interest to all parties

questions.exp: When a licensee has a personal financial interest in a transaction — whether buying for themselves, their family, or a business entity they control — they must disclose their licensed status and the nature of their interest. Failure to disclose is a violation of license law.

questions.q: Internet advertising by Pennsylvania licensees must include:

opts.A: The brokerage firm's name and the state where licensed
opts.B: The property's MLS number
opts.C: The licensee's photo and years of experience
opts.D: The listing price and commission rate

questions.exp: Pennsylvania advertising regulations require that online advertising (websites, social media, email) clearly identify the brokerage firm name and the state in which the licensee is licensed. Personal advertising that does not identify the brokerage violates the rules.

questions.q: A "pocket listing" (off-market listing) creates potential ethical concerns because:

opts.A: It violates RESPA's disclosure requirements
opts.B: It is always illegal under state license law
opts.C: It may limit market exposure and fail to serve the seller's best interests
opts.D: It requires a special license endorsement

questions.exp: A pocket listing is marketed only within an agent's personal network, bypassing the MLS. While sometimes legitimate (at the seller's request), it can reduce competition and result in a lower sale price, potentially breaching the agent's duty of loyalty and best-efforts representation to the seller.

questions.q: A broker who receives compensation from both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction without both parties' knowledge and consent is guilty of:

opts.A: Undisclosed dual compensation (a license law violation)
opts.B: Conversion
opts.C: Commingling
opts.D: Conspiracy

questions.exp: Receiving compensation from both buyer and seller without full disclosure and written consent from both parties is prohibited under Pennsylvania license law. It is a form of undisclosed dual agency that harms both parties and violates the agent's fiduciary obligations.

questions.q: The broker's duty to present offers continues:

opts.A: Only until the first offer is accepted
opts.B: Only during business hours
opts.C: Until closing, unless the seller instructs otherwise in writing
opts.D: Only until the listing agreement expires

questions.exp: A listing broker must continue to submit all offers and counter-offers objectively until closing, unless the seller has given written instruction to the contrary. Even after a contract is signed, backup offers may be required to be submitted if the seller wishes.

questions.q: When a salesperson moves from one broker to another, which document formally transfers the license?

opts.A: A letter of resignation to the old broker
opts.B: A transfer application filed with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission
opts.C: A new license exam score
opts.D: An MLS membership transfer form

questions.exp: To officially transfer a license between brokers in Pennsylvania, the licensee must file a transfer application with the Pennsylvania Real Estate Commission (usually online). The licensee cannot lawfully engage in real estate activities for the new broker until the Commission processes the transfer.

questions.q: A "teaser" or "bait and switch" advertisement is prohibited because it:

opts.A: Promises a listing price below market value
opts.B: Uses photos of properties not owned by the agent
opts.C: Advertises a property or price that is not genuinely available to attract clients, then directs them to different properties
opts.D: Fails to include the commission rate in the ad

questions.exp: Bait-and-switch advertising attracts clients with an attractive but unavailable or misrepresented offer, then redirects them to other properties. It violates RESPA, FTC regulations, and Pennsylvania license law as deceptive advertising.

questions.q: Which of the following actions by a licensee constitutes "conversion" of client funds?

opts.A: Depositing earnest money in the escrow account immediately
opts.B: Investing escrow funds in a money market account
opts.C: Holding earnest money until closing
opts.D: Using escrowed client funds for personal expenses

questions.exp: Conversion is the unauthorized use of another's funds — for example, using client escrow money for personal or business expenses. It is more serious than commingling and may constitute fraud or embezzlement, in addition to license law violations.

questions.q: An agent representing a seller receives an offer that the agent believes is too low. The agent should:

opts.A: Reject the offer on the seller's behalf without presenting it
opts.B: Present the offer to the seller and let the seller decide
opts.C: Counter the offer without consulting the seller
opts.D: Ask the buyer's agent to submit a higher offer first

questions.exp: A listing agent has a fiduciary duty to present all offers to the seller promptly, regardless of price. The decision to accept, reject, or counter is the seller's alone to make. An agent who screens or delays offers based on personal judgment violates their duty.

questions.q: A "buyer's premium" at auction is:

opts.A: A bonus paid by the seller to the high bidder
opts.B: A commission paid from escrow to the buyer's agent
opts.C: A fee the buyer pays to reserve a property before auction
opts.D: An additional amount above the winning bid paid by the buyer to the auctioneer

questions.exp: In real estate auctions, a buyer's premium is a percentage added to the winning bid that goes to the auction company. For example, a 10% buyer's premium on a $200,000 winning bid means the buyer pays $220,000 total. The seller typically receives only the hammer (bid) price.

questions.q: In a real estate transaction, a fiduciary relationship exists between:

opts.A: The agent and the principal (client)
opts.B: The seller and the buyer
opts.C: The listing agent and the buyer
opts.D: The agent and the cooperating agent

questions.exp: A fiduciary relationship is one of trust and confidence. In real estate, it exists between the agent (broker/salesperson) and their principal (client — the party who hired them). The agent owes fiduciary duties of loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, obedience, accounting, and reasonable care to the client.

questions.q: The duty of LOYALTY requires an agent to:

opts.A: Place the client's interests above all others, including the agent's own
opts.B: Account for all monies received
opts.C: Follow all of the client's lawful instructions
opts.D: Provide accurate and current information to the client

questions.exp: The duty of loyalty requires the agent to subordinate their personal interests and the interests of any third party to the client's best interests. This includes not taking secret profits, not representing adverse parties without disclosure, and not acting to the client's detriment.

questions.q: Which type of agency is created when an agent's actions appear authorized even without an express grant of authority?

opts.A: Apparent (ostensible) agency
opts.B: Implied agency
opts.C: Express agency
opts.D: Dual agency

questions.exp: Apparent agency (ostensible agency) arises when the principal's conduct leads a third party to reasonably believe that an agent has authority — even if no actual authority was granted. The principal can be bound by the agent's acts if they created the appearance of authority.

questions.q: A buyer's agent owes fiduciary duties to the buyer. Which of the following does NOT violate the agent's duty to the buyer?

opts.A: Disclosing the buyer's maximum price to the seller
opts.B: Negotiating a price higher than the buyer wants to pay
opts.C: Disclosing to the seller known material defects in the property (factual information)
opts.D: Encouraging the buyer to overpay for the property

questions.exp: Even a buyer's agent must disclose known material defects (facts) to sellers or other parties — this is a legal obligation overriding the agency relationship. However, disclosing the buyer's negotiating position, maximum price, or motivation would breach the duty of confidentiality to the buyer.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, a licensee representing both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction is engaging in:

opts.A: Designated agency
opts.B: Sub-agency
opts.C: Dual agency
opts.D: Implied agency

questions.exp: Dual agency occurs when the same agent (or broker) represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction. It creates an inherent conflict of interest because the agent cannot fully advocate for both parties simultaneously. In Pennsylvania, dual agency requires written informed consent from both parties.

questions.q: Designated agency in Pennsylvania allows:

opts.A: One agent to represent both parties without disclosure
opts.B: The broker to split commissions between two MLS members
opts.C: A broker in one state to represent clients in another state
opts.D: Two different salespersons within the same brokerage to represent the buyer and seller separately

questions.exp: Designated agency is a mechanism to address in-house transactions: the broker designates one licensee to represent the buyer and a different licensee to represent the seller. Each designated agent may represent their client fully, while the broker acts as a neutral dual agent. Written consent is required.

questions.q: A sub-agent is BEST described as:

opts.A: An assistant to a buyer's agent
opts.B: An unlicensed transaction coordinator
opts.C: An agent of the listing broker who owes fiduciary duties to the seller
opts.D: A buyer's agent working without a written agreement

questions.exp: A sub-agent is a cooperating broker/agent who works with a buyer but represents the seller (through the listing broker). The sub-agent owes fiduciary duties to the seller — not to the buyer. Sub-agency has declined significantly due to buyer agency and confusion about representation.

questions.q: A transaction broker (facilitator) in Pennsylvania:

opts.A: Owes full fiduciary duties to both buyer and seller
opts.B: Represents neither party and has no duty of care
opts.C: Is not permitted under Pennsylvania law
opts.D: Assists the transaction without representing either party as a fiduciary

questions.exp: A transaction broker (or facilitator) assists the buyer and seller in completing the transaction without representing either party as a client with full fiduciary duties. The transaction broker still owes duties of honesty, disclosure of material facts, and reasonable skill — but not full loyalty to either side.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an agent exceeding their authority (acting outside the scope of agency)?

opts.A: Presenting the seller's counteroffer to the buyer
opts.B: Showing the property on a Sunday
opts.C: Accepting an offer on behalf of the seller without authorization
opts.D: Ordering a home inspection for the buyer

questions.exp: A listing agent has authority to market the property, present offers, and facilitate negotiations — but does NOT have authority to accept an offer on behalf of the seller unless specifically granted (through a power of attorney or explicit written authority). Acceptance requires the principal's consent.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes the duty of "obedience" in an agency relationship?

opts.A: Following any instruction, whether legal or not
opts.B: Informing the principal of all material facts
opts.C: Following the principal's lawful instructions, even if the agent disagrees
opts.D: Disclosing all known facts to the other party

questions.exp: The duty of obedience requires the agent to follow the client's lawful and ethical instructions. The agent may disagree but must comply unless the instruction is illegal or unethical. If the instruction is illegal (e.g., fair housing violation), the agent must refuse.

questions.q: An agent's duty of CONFIDENTIALITY means the agent must NOT disclose:

opts.A: The property's physical condition to the buyer
opts.B: The seller's motivation for selling (unless the seller authorizes disclosure)
opts.C: The existence of other offers to the buyer
opts.D: The property's listing price to prospective buyers

questions.exp: The duty of confidentiality requires protecting the principal's private information — including their motivation for selling, financial circumstances, urgency, and negotiating position — unless the principal authorizes disclosure. This duty continues even after the agency relationship ends.

questions.q: An agent has a duty to DISCLOSE to a buyer which of the following?

opts.A: The seller's rock-bottom acceptable price
opts.B: Material defects in the property known to the agent
opts.C: That the seller has received another offer (but not the terms)
opts.D: The seller's personal reason for relocating

questions.exp: An agent representing the seller (or acting as a dual agent) must disclose known material defects to the buyer — this is a duty to the public that overrides agency considerations. However, the seller's confidential negotiating position (rock-bottom price, personal motivation) must remain confidential.

questions.q: The duty of ACCOUNTING requires an agent to:

opts.A: Account for all money and property received on the principal's behalf
opts.B: Audit the brokerage's financial statements
opts.C: Prepare tax returns for the principal
opts.D: Provide the principal with a monthly profit-and-loss statement

questions.exp: The duty of accounting requires the agent to maintain careful records of all funds received and disbursed on behalf of the principal — including earnest money, rents collected, and expenses paid. Funds must be held in proper escrow accounts and reported accurately.

questions.q: An agency relationship may be terminated by all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: Mutual agreement of agent and principal
opts.B: Completion of the transaction (purpose achieved)
opts.C: Death of either party
opts.D: The principal deciding to accept a lower offer

questions.exp: Agency terminates upon: completion of the purpose, mutual agreement, expiration of the term, revocation by the principal, renunciation by the agent, death or incapacity of either party, or destruction of the subject property. A principal accepting an offer does not terminate the agency — the agent continues working until closing.

questions.q: Implied agency may be accidentally created when:

opts.A: A buyer signs a buyer representation agreement
opts.B: A licensee performs agency-type tasks for a party who has not signed a representation agreement
opts.C: A seller signs a listing agreement
opts.D: An agent shows a listed property to a buyer

questions.exp: Implied agency arises from the conduct of the parties rather than a written agreement. If a licensee provides advice, negotiating assistance, or other services that a reasonable person would associate with representation — without disclosing the absence of a formal agency — an implied agency relationship may be created, with all its fiduciary obligations.

questions.q: Under Pennsylvania's agency law, an agent may represent a client against their own interests if:

opts.A: The agent discloses the conflict at the end of the transaction
opts.B: The commission is split with the other party
opts.C: The broker instructs the agent to proceed
opts.D: Both parties give informed written consent to dual agency

questions.exp: Acting against a client's interests is generally a breach of fiduciary duty. The exception is dual agency — representing both buyer and seller — which is permissible in Pennsylvania only if both parties are fully informed of the conflict and consent in writing. Without consent, dual agency violates the agent's fiduciary obligations.

questions.q: When an agent acts outside the scope of their authority and the principal ratifies the act, the principal:

opts.A: May sue the agent for the unauthorized act
opts.B: Becomes bound by the agent's unauthorized act
opts.C: Has no responsibility for the agent's actions
opts.D: Must dismiss the agent from the agency relationship

questions.exp: Ratification occurs when a principal, after learning that their agent acted without authority, chooses to accept and approve the act. By ratifying, the principal adopts the unauthorized act as their own, as if the agent had original authority. The principal is then bound.

questions.q: The Consumer Notice required in Pennsylvania agency law must be provided:

opts.A: At closing, for the buyer to sign
opts.B: At the first substantive contact with a potential buyer or seller
opts.C: Only if the consumer requests it in writing
opts.D: Only after a listing agreement has been signed

questions.exp: Pennsylvania regulations require that licensees provide the Consumer Notice (explaining types of agency relationships, duties, and required disclosures) at the first substantive contact with a prospective buyer or seller — before any significant discussion of real estate.

questions.q: A buyer's agent who learns that the seller is in financial distress and must sell quickly should:

opts.A: Use this information to benefit the buyer in negotiations (within ethical limits)
opts.B: Ignore the information as irrelevant to the transaction
opts.C: Disclose this to the seller as a courtesy
opts.D: Report this information to the MLS

questions.exp: A buyer's agent has a duty of loyalty to the buyer. Information about the seller's motivation, financial distress, or urgency benefits the buyer in negotiations and should be used — not disclosed to the seller or ignored. This is a core function of buyer representation.

questions.q: The "reasonable care" duty requires an agent to:

opts.A: Guarantee that the property will appreciate in value
opts.B: Perform tasks that no other agent could match
opts.C: Perform duties perfectly without any errors
opts.D: Exercise the level of skill and care expected of a competent real estate professional

questions.exp: The duty of reasonable care (skill and diligence) requires the agent to perform their duties with the competence expected of a reasonably skilled real estate professional. It does not require perfection but does require the agent to stay informed, be competent, and act diligently on the client's behalf.

questions.q: The federal Fair Housing Act of 1968 prohibits discrimination based on all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: Occupation
opts.B: National origin and religion
opts.C: Sex (gender)
opts.D: Race and color

questions.exp: The federal Fair Housing Act's seven protected classes are: race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status, and disability. Occupation is NOT a federally protected class. However, some state and local laws protect additional classes such as sexual orientation and source of income.

questions.q: Steering is the illegal practice of:

opts.A: Refusing to make loans in certain neighborhoods
opts.B: Inducing panic selling by suggesting minority groups are moving in
opts.C: Setting different sales prices for different buyers
opts.D: Directing buyers toward or away from certain neighborhoods based on protected class characteristics

questions.exp: Steering occurs when an agent guides buyers toward or away from certain neighborhoods based on their race, national origin, religion, or other protected class.
