It perpetuates segregation and violates the Fair Housing Act, even when the agent believes they are acting in the buyer's interest.

questions.q: Which federal law added "familial status" and "disability" as protected classes to the Fair Housing Act?

opts.A: Civil Rights Act of 1964
opts.B: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
opts.C: Fair Housing Act of 1968
opts.D: Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990

questions.exp: The Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988 expanded the original Fair Housing Act's protections by adding familial status (households with children under 18, pregnant women) and disability (physical or mental impairment that substantially limits major life activities) as protected classes.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act, "familial status" protects:

opts.A: Married couples only
opts.B: Adults over age 55 living alone
opts.C: Households with children under 18, including pregnant women and those seeking custody
opts.D: Only single-parent households

questions.exp: Familial status protection covers households that include one or more individuals under 18 under the custody of a parent or legal guardian, pregnant women, and those in the process of securing legal custody of a minor. Housing for older persons (55+) communities may qualify for an exemption.

questions.q: A seller instructs the listing agent: "Don't show my house to anyone with children — I don't want the floors scratched." The agent should:

opts.A: Refuse the instruction and explain that it violates the Fair Housing Act
opts.B: Note the instruction in the listing file and follow it
opts.C: Comply with the seller's instructions since the seller has the right to sell to whomever they choose
opts.D: Accept the listing but disregard the instruction quietly

questions.exp: Refusing to show property to families with children discriminates based on familial status — a protected class. The agent may not follow this instruction. The agent should explain that compliance would violate the Fair Housing Act and, if the seller insists, the agent should decline the listing.

questions.q: An exemption to the federal Fair Housing Act permits discrimination by:

opts.A: Any private homeowner who lives in a single-family home
opts.B: Any landlord who rents fewer than three units
opts.C: Religious organizations renting to members only, for any type of property
opts.D: An owner of a single-family home who sells without a broker and without discriminatory advertising

questions.exp: The "Mrs. Murphy" exemption permits an owner of a single-family home to sell or rent without complying with the Fair Housing Act IF: they own no more than three single-family homes, do not use a broker, and do not use discriminatory advertising. Owners of owner-occupied buildings with four or fewer units (Mrs. Murphy exemption) may also be exempt for rentals. Religious and private club exemptions have limitations.

questions.q: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) prohibits discrimination in lending based on all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: Race and color
opts.B: Credit score
opts.C: Age (provided the applicant is old enough to enter a contract)
opts.D: Sex and marital status

questions.exp: ECOA prohibits lending discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age (if old enough to contract), and receipt of public assistance. Credit score is not a protected class — lenders may lawfully consider creditworthiness as a business decision.

questions.q: An Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accommodation requirement for commercial properties requires owners to:

opts.A: Remove barriers to access in public accommodations when readily achievable
opts.B: Remodel residential homes for accessibility
opts.C: Provide housing vouchers for disabled tenants
opts.D: Install elevators in all commercial buildings regardless of cost

questions.exp: The ADA requires that public accommodations (businesses open to the public) remove architectural barriers when it is "readily achievable" — meaning easily accomplishable without much difficulty or expense. The ADA applies to commercial properties and places of public accommodation, not residential housing (which is covered by the Fair Housing Act).

questions.q: A disabled tenant requests permission to install grab bars in the bathroom of a rental unit. Under the Fair Housing Act, the landlord must:

opts.A: Allow the modification at the tenant's expense, and may require restoration upon lease end
opts.B: Pay for the modification
opts.C: Refuse because alterations damage the property
opts.D: Allow it only if other tenants agree

questions.exp: Under the Fair Housing Act, landlords must allow disabled tenants to make reasonable modifications to the unit at the tenant's expense. The landlord may condition approval on the tenant's promise to restore the property to its original condition (where reasonable) when they move out.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act, which of the following is a "reasonable accommodation" a landlord must provide?

opts.A: Allowing a disabled tenant to keep an assistance animal in a no-pets building
opts.B: Reducing the rent by 50% for a disabled tenant
opts.C: Installing a swimming pool for a disabled tenant
opts.D: Providing a unit on the first floor to any tenant who requests one

questions.exp: Reasonable accommodations are changes in rules, policies, practices, or services that a landlord must make for a disabled person. Allowing an assistance (service or emotional support) animal in a no-pets building is a classic example — the pet policy must yield to the disability need. A landlord may not charge a pet deposit for a bona fide assistance animal.

questions.q: Pennsylvania's Human Relations Act (PHRA) adds which classes of protection beyond the federal Fair Housing Act?

opts.A: Pet ownership and income level
opts.B: Age only
opts.C: Age, ancestry, and use of a guide animal, among others
opts.D: Sexual orientation and credit history

questions.exp: The Pennsylvania Human Relations Act adds additional protected classes beyond the federal law, including age, ancestry, and the use of a guide dog or support animal. PHRA enforcement is through the Pennsylvania Human Relations Commission (PHRC).

questions.q: A complainant who believes they have been discriminated against under the federal Fair Housing Act must generally file a complaint with HUD within:

opts.A: 90 days of the discriminatory act
opts.B: 6 months of the discriminatory act
opts.C: 1 year of the discriminatory act
opts.D: 2 years of the discriminatory act

questions.exp: A complaint under the federal Fair Housing Act must be filed with HUD within one year of the alleged discriminatory act. Alternatively, the complainant may file a private lawsuit in federal court within two years. The statute of limitations is important for preserving rights.

questions.q: Which civil rights law made it illegal to discriminate in ALL property sales, not just in federally assisted housing, based on race and national origin — and has NO exemptions?

opts.A: Fair Housing Act of 1968
opts.B: Civil Rights Act of 1964
opts.C: Fair Housing Amendments Act of 1988
opts.D: Civil Rights Act of 1866 (42 U.S.C. § 1982)

questions.exp: The Civil Rights Act of 1866 guarantees all citizens the right to inherit, purchase, lease, sell, hold, and convey real and personal property — and has NO exemptions for any type of property or seller. After Jones v. Mayer (1968), this law was reaffirmed and applies to all private sales based on race.

questions.q: In an "55 and older" housing community, what percentage of units must be occupied by at least one person 55 or older?
questions.exp: Under the Housing for Older Persons Act (HOPA), a qualifying 55+ community must have at least 80% of occupied units with at least one resident who is 55 or older, publish and follow policies that demonstrate intent to be senior housing, and comply with HUD verification requirements.

questions.q: An agent who uses different qualification standards for buyers based on their national origin is violating:

opts.A: Only the Civil Rights Act of 1866
opts.B: The Fair Housing Act and potentially ECOA
opts.C: Only ECOA
opts.D: Only Pennsylvania Human Relations Act

questions.exp: Applying different qualification standards (e.g., requiring larger down payments or different credit criteria) based on a buyer's national origin violates both the Fair Housing Act (in the sale or lease of housing) and ECOA (if applied to lending). Both federal laws prohibit this form of discrimination.

questions.q: Which of the following advertising practices violates the Fair Housing Act?

opts.A: Describing the home's square footage and features
opts.B: Using models of only one race in advertising photos for a development
opts.C: Advertising in a local newspaper
opts.D: Stating the school district the property is located in

questions.exp: HUD's advertising guidelines prohibit using models of a single race in advertising, as it signals that only people of that race are welcome. Fair housing advertising must use diverse models and may not include statements, phrases, or images that signal a preference for or against any protected class.

questions.q: The maximum civil penalty for a first violation of the Fair Housing Act (non-private lawsuit, HUD administrative case) is approximately:

opts.D: $21,000–$25,000 (periodically adjusted by HUD)

questions.exp: Civil penalties for Fair Housing Act violations in HUD administrative proceedings are adjusted periodically for inflation. For a first violation they have typically been in the range of $21,000–$25,000; subsequent violations carry higher penalties. Private lawsuit damages are unlimited (actual + punitive).

questions.q: A real estate agent who tells prospective white buyers that a neighborhood is "changing" (implying minority residents are moving in) to induce quick sales is committing:

opts.A: Steering
opts.B: Dual agency
opts.C: Redlining
opts.D: Blockbusting

questions.exp: Blockbusting (panic peddling) is the illegal practice of inducing owners — usually in a targeted neighborhood — to sell their homes by suggesting that members of a protected class are moving in, which will cause the neighborhood to decline. It is prohibited by the Fair Housing Act.

questions.q: Fair housing testing involves:

opts.A: Administering real estate knowledge exams to agents
opts.B: Surveying residents about neighborhood satisfaction
opts.C: Sending matched testers (who differ only in protected class) to detect discriminatory practices
opts.D: Requiring all listings to be shown to at least five different buyers

questions.exp: Fair housing tests use matched pairs of testers — identical in every respect except a protected characteristic (race, disability, familial status, etc.) — to test whether agents or landlords treat them differently. Test results have been admitted as evidence in Fair Housing Act enforcement cases.

questions.q: Under the Fair Housing Act, which of the following statements made by a seller is LEGAL?

opts.A: "I won't sell to anyone with children."
opts.B: "I prefer buyers from my own country."
opts.C: "I need to close within 30 days."
opts.D: "Show this only to buyers who speak English."

questions.exp: A seller is entitled to specify lawful transaction requirements — such as a closing date, price, financing terms, or inspection conditions. Requiring a specific closing date is not discriminatory. The other options discriminate based on familial status, national origin, or national origin/language — all protected classes.

questions.q: An exclusive right-to-sell listing gives the listing broker the right to a commission:

opts.A: Only if the broker personally finds the buyer
opts.B: Only if another broker brings the buyer through the MLS
opts.C: Only if the property sells above the listing price
opts.D: Regardless of who sells the property, including the owner

questions.exp: In an exclusive right-to-sell listing, the listing broker earns a commission if the property is sold during the listing period — no matter who finds the buyer, including the seller themselves. This is the listing type that gives brokers the strongest protection and is most commonly used.

questions.q: An exclusive agency listing allows the seller to:

opts.A: List with multiple brokers simultaneously
opts.B: Cancel the listing at any time without obligation
opts.C: Sell the property themselves without paying the listing broker a commission
opts.D: Negotiate the commission rate after the sale

questions.exp: In an exclusive agency listing, the seller retains the right to sell the property themselves, without owing a commission to the listing broker, if the seller personally finds the buyer. If any broker (including the listing broker) finds the buyer, a commission is owed to the listing broker.

questions.q: In an open listing, the seller may:

opts.A: List with multiple brokers and pay only the one who brings the buyer
opts.B: Never sell the property without using an agent
opts.C: List only with a single MLS-member broker
opts.D: Set the commission at a flat dollar amount for all brokers

questions.exp: An open listing is a non-exclusive arrangement where the seller may list with any number of brokers simultaneously and pays a commission only to the broker who produces the buyer. If the seller sells the property themselves, no commission is owed to anyone.

questions.q: Which type of listing is MOST commonly submitted to the MLS and recommended by most real estate associations?

opts.A: Open listing
opts.B: Exclusive right-to-sell listing
opts.C: Exclusive agency listing
opts.D: Net listing

questions.exp: The exclusive right-to-sell listing is the industry standard and the listing type preferred by brokers. MLS rules typically require this type for full cooperation. It provides the strongest incentive for brokers to actively market the property, since they earn the commission regardless of who produces the buyer.

questions.q: A listing agreement is a contract between the seller and:

opts.A: The broker (brokerage firm)
opts.B: The buyer's agent
opts.C: The listing salesperson
opts.D: The MLS

questions.exp: The listing agreement is a contract between the property owner (seller) and the broker (brokerage firm). Individual salespersons may sign on behalf of their broker, but the legal contract is between the seller and the brokerage. The salesperson is an agent of the broker, not a contracting party.

questions.q: A listing agreement MUST include which of the following to be valid and enforceable in Pennsylvania?

opts.A: A guaranteed selling price
opts.B: A maximum commission cap
opts.C: The buyer's anticipated financing terms
opts.D: A definite expiration date

questions.exp: Pennsylvania law requires that all listing agreements contain a definite expiration date. Without a specific end date, the listing may be considered unenforceable or create disputes about its duration. Open-ended listings are not permitted under RELRA.

questions.q: An "override clause" (extender/carry-over clause) in a listing agreement is intended to:

opts.A: Allow the broker to extend the listing unilaterally
opts.B: Protect the broker's commission if a buyer found during the listing period buys the property shortly after expiration
opts.C: Increase the commission rate after expiration
opts.D: Override the seller's rejection of an offer

questions.exp: An override (extender or carry-over) clause entitles the broker to a commission for a set period after the listing expires if the property is sold to a buyer who was introduced to the property during the listing period. This protects the broker from sellers waiting for expiration to avoid paying commission.

questions.q: The listing price is determined by:

opts.A: The listing broker based on what the market will bear
opts.B: The seller, based on advice from the broker and market data
opts.C: The county tax assessment
opts.D: The MLS board of directors

questions.exp: The listing price is the seller's decision. The broker provides a comparative market analysis (CMA) and professional advice, but the final listing price belongs to the seller. The broker does not set the price unilaterally.

questions.q: Under the MLS, if a listing is "Active Under Contract" (AUC), it means:

opts.A: The property has been sold and recorded
opts.B: The property is available for showings with no pending offer
opts.C: The property has an accepted offer but the listing remains visible (e.g., accepting backup offers)
opts.D: The listing has been canceled by the seller

questions.exp: The "Active Under Contract" MLS status indicates a contract has been accepted, but the listing broker continues to show the property and accept backup offers. It differs from "Under Contract" (which shows the property as effectively off the market) and from "Sold" (which indicates closing has occurred).

questions.q: A seller who cancels a listing agreement before its expiration date may be liable to the broker for:

opts.A: The full commission as if the property had sold
opts.B: Nothing, since sellers have the right to cancel at any time
opts.C: The broker's actual out-of-pocket marketing expenses
opts.D: A penalty of one percent of the listing price

questions.exp: If a seller unilaterally cancels a valid listing agreement before expiration, the broker may have a claim for actual expenses incurred (advertising, photography, MLS fees) — not necessarily the full commission, unless a specific cancellation fee was agreed upon. The commission is typically owed only if a ready, willing, and able buyer is produced.

questions.q: A property listed by Broker A is shown by Broker B to a buyer, who then purchases it. In this cooperation, Broker A is the:

opts.A: Cooperating (selling) broker
opts.B: Listing broker
opts.C: Buyer's agent
opts.D: Sub-agent of Broker B

questions.exp: Broker A, who has the listing agreement with the seller, is the listing broker. Broker B (who brought the buyer) is the cooperating broker (sometimes called the selling broker). The commission is typically split between them per the MLS offer of cooperation.

questions.q: Before signing a listing agreement, the licensee should conduct a CMA to:

opts.A: Determine the property tax assessment
opts.B: Calculate the broker's commission
opts.C: Satisfy the lender's requirements for the seller's existing mortgage
opts.D: Recommend a market-appropriate listing price and help the seller understand current market conditions

questions.exp: A CMA (Comparative Market Analysis) compares the subject property to recently sold comparable properties to suggest a competitive listing price range. It is a fundamental tool that helps the seller price realistically and understand buyer expectations in the current market.

questions.q: A seller who grants a buyer an option to purchase but also lists the property with a broker creates a potential conflict if:

opts.A: The optionee exercises the option during the listing period and both the optionee and the broker claim conflicting rights
opts.B: The listing agreement has a carry-over clause
opts.C: The MLS requires exclusive listings
opts.D: The option price is above the listing price

questions.exp: If the optionee exercises the option during an active exclusive right-to-sell listing, the broker may claim a commission (since a sale occurred during the listing period), while the seller may dispute owing a commission on a pre-existing option. These conflicts should be addressed in the listing agreement or the option agreement.

questions.q: Which of the following would be an example of a material fact that a listing agent must disclose to potential buyers?

opts.A: The seller's asking price strategy
opts.B: The seller's next home purchase
opts.C: A leaking basement that the agent observed during a walk-through
opts.D: The seller's willingness to carry financing

questions.exp: A material defect that affects the property's value, habitability, or safety — such as a leaking basement — must be disclosed by the listing agent. Sellers' private motivations and confidential negotiating positions are not material facts requiring disclosure.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, all listing agreements for residential real estate must be:

opts.A: In writing (Statute of Frauds)
opts.B: Filed with the county recorder within 10 days
opts.C: Notarized by a public notary
opts.D: Reviewed by the seller's attorney before signing

questions.exp: Pennsylvania's Statute of Frauds requires listing agreements (employment contracts between broker and seller) to be in writing and signed to be enforceable. An oral listing agreement generally cannot be enforced to collect a commission. Attorney review is recommended but not legally required.

questions.q: A buyer's representation agreement differs from a listing agreement in that it:

opts.A: Is not required to be in writing
opts.B: Is between the buyer and the MLS
opts.C: Creates an agency relationship between the buyer and the broker
opts.D: Sets the listing price for the property

questions.exp: A buyer representation (buyer agency) agreement is a contract between the buyer and the broker establishing the broker as the buyer's agent. Like a listing agreement, it creates an agency relationship — but on the buyer's side of the transaction.

questions.q: A safety clause in a listing agreement protects the broker by:

opts.A: Insuring the broker against E&O claims
opts.B: Limiting the broker's liability for property defects
opts.C: Allowing the broker to refuse unsafe showing requests
opts.D: Entitling the broker to a commission if a buyer shown the property during the listing period purchases it after expiration

questions.exp: The safety (protection, override, or extender) clause entitles the broker to a commission for a specified time after the listing expires if the property is sold to a buyer who was introduced to the property during the listing period. The broker must typically submit a list of such prospects at or near the listing's expiration.

questions.q: Which of the following terms in a listing agreement is NEGOTIABLE between the seller and broker?

opts.A: The seller's legal name
opts.B: The commission rate
opts.C: The property's tax parcel number
opts.D: The property's legal description

questions.exp: Commission rates are negotiable between sellers and brokers — there is no legally mandated rate. Antitrust law (Sherman Act) prohibits price-fixing among competing brokers. The property's legal description, seller's name, and tax parcel number are factual matters that are not negotiable.

questions.q: A seller asks the listing agent to withhold disclosure of a known leaking roof from buyers "to get a better price." The agent should:

opts.A: Follow the seller's instructions since the seller is the client
opts.B: Disclose only to buyers who specifically ask about the roof
opts.C: Place the information in the MLS remarks but not tell buyers directly
opts.D: Refuse the instruction — a known material defect must be disclosed

questions.exp: An agent may not conceal or misrepresent a known material defect, even at the seller's instruction. The duty to disclose material facts to buyers is a legal obligation (PA Seller Disclosure Law, license law, common law) that overrides the agent's duty of obedience to the seller when the instruction is illegal or unethical.

questions.q: An agent who lists a property at a price higher than the CMA suggests in order to win the listing (and then later pressures the seller to reduce the price) is engaging in:

opts.A: "Buying the listing" (overpricing to obtain the listing)
opts.B: Fair market analysis
opts.C: Good faith pricing strategy
opts.D: Standard MLS practice

questions.exp: "Buying the listing" refers to an agent suggesting an unrealistically high listing price to persuade a seller to sign the listing agreement (flattering the seller's ego), with the knowledge that price reductions will follow. It is an unethical practice that ultimately harms the seller by causing the property to sit on the market and eventually sell for less.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Association of REALTORS® (PAR) Standard Agreement for the Sale of Real Estate is a:

opts.A: Legal guarantee of the property's condition
opts.B: Contract form that must be approved by the Real Estate Commission for each use
opts.C: Binding offer form that sellers must sign within 24 hours
opts.D: Pre-printed form that licensees may complete without engaging in the unauthorized practice of law

questions.exp: The PAR Standard Agreement is an approved, pre-printed contract form that Pennsylvania licensees may fill in on behalf of their clients. Because it is a pre-drafted form, completing it does not constitute unauthorized practice of law — as long as the licensee does not draft custom legal provisions.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common contingency in a residential sales contract?

opts.A: Seller's acceptance of any buyer offer
opts.B: Broker's approval of the transaction
opts.C: MLS ratification of the sale price
opts.D: Buyer's ability to obtain financing at specified terms

questions.exp: A mortgage (financing) contingency allows the buyer to exit the contract without penalty if they cannot obtain a loan at the interest rate, loan amount, and terms specified in the contract. Other common contingencies include home inspection, sale of the buyer's current home, and appraisal.

questions.q: An inspection contingency gives the buyer the right to:

opts.A: Move into the property before closing
opts.B: Negotiate a price reduction without grounds
opts.C: Have the property professionally inspected and negotiate repairs or withdraw based on the findings
opts.D: Require the seller to make all repairs found by any inspector

questions.exp: An inspection contingency allows the buyer to hire a licensed inspector. Based on the report, the buyer may request repairs or credits, accept the property as-is, or withdraw from the contract if the defects are material. The buyer does not automatically have the right to demand all repairs — the seller may negotiate or decline.

questions.q: In a sales contract, the phrase "time is of the essence" means:

opts.A: The transaction must close within one week
opts.B: All deadlines in the contract are strictly enforced
opts.C: Both parties must sign the contract on the same day
opts.D: The seller must vacate before the closing date

questions.exp: When a contract states "time is of the essence," all deadlines — including inspection periods, contingency removal dates, and the closing date — are strictly binding. Missing a deadline can constitute a material breach of contract, potentially allowing the other party to terminate.

questions.q: A home sale contingency allows the buyer to:

opts.A: Purchase the property only if the seller agrees to a price reduction
opts.B: Cancel the contract if the buyer's existing home does not sell within the contingency period
opts.C: List their current home with the seller's listing agent
opts.D: Move out of their current home before the closing date

questions.exp: A home sale contingency makes the purchase of a new home contingent on the buyer selling their current home within a specified time. If the buyer's home does not sell, they may exit the contract. Sellers often include a "kick-out" (bump) clause allowing them to keep marketing and accept other offers.

questions.q: The appraisal contingency in a sales contract protects the buyer by:

opts.A: Allowing the buyer to renegotiate or withdraw if the appraised value is less than the purchase price
opts.B: Allowing the buyer to terminate if the property is overbuilt for the neighborhood
opts.C: Requiring the appraiser to value the property at least at the purchase price
opts.D: Requiring the lender to fund the loan regardless of appraised value

questions.exp: If the property appraises below the contract price, the buyer's lender typically won't lend more than the appraised value. An appraisal contingency gives the buyer the right to renegotiate the price, make up the difference in cash, or exit the contract without losing the earnest money.

questions.q: The "as of" date in a real estate sales contract is important because it:

opts.A: Sets the date the seller must vacate
opts.B: Establishes when the contract's rights and obligations begin
opts.C: Determines when the buyer takes possession
opts.D: Sets the final date for financing contingency removal

questions.exp: The effective ("as of") date is the date from which contract deadlines, contingency periods, and obligations are measured. It is typically the date of the last party's signature accepting the contract (mutual execution), not just the date the offer was written.

questions.q: Personal property items (e.g., refrigerator, washer/dryer) included in a sale should be:

opts.A: Assumed to transfer with the real estate automatically
opts.B: Listed only in the seller's disclosure form
opts.C: Explicitly identified and included in the sales contract
opts.D: Transferred by a separate bill of sale filed with the county

questions.exp: Personal property (chattel) does not automatically transfer with real property — it must be specifically named in the sales contract to be included in the sale. Without written inclusion, the seller may legally remove appliances, light fixtures (if not affixed), and other items before closing.

questions.q: If a buyer and seller agree to a price reduction after the initial contract is signed, this change must be documented by:

opts.A: A verbal agreement between both parties
opts.B: A text message from the listing agent
opts.C: A written addendum or amendment signed by both parties
opts.D: A MLS status change by the listing broker

questions.exp: Any modification to a real estate contract — including price reductions, closing date changes, or added terms — must be in writing and signed by all parties to be enforceable (Statute of Frauds). Verbal modifications to a written real estate contract are generally unenforceable.

questions.q: When a buyer makes an offer with an escalation clause, it means the buyer:

opts.A: Agrees to outbid any competing offer up to a stated maximum price
opts.B: Agrees to pay all closing costs above a set amount
opts.C: Guarantees to pay any price the seller requests
opts.D: Allows the seller to change the price after acceptance

questions.exp: An escalation clause automatically increases a buyer's offer by a set increment above any competing offer, up to a specified maximum ("cap"). For example: "I offer $300,000, and will beat any competing offer by $5,000, up to a maximum of $330,000." It is common in competitive markets.

questions.q: Seller concessions in a real estate transaction refer to:

opts.A: The seller's agreement to repair all defects before closing
opts.B: The seller's agreement to reduce the commission
opts.C: The seller's willingness to vacate before closing
opts.D: The seller's agreement to pay a portion of the buyer's closing costs

questions.exp: Seller concessions (or seller-paid closing costs) occur when the seller agrees to pay a portion of the buyer's closing costs as part of the negotiated terms. Lenders cap the amount of concessions allowed (e.g., 3-6% of the purchase price for conventional loans) to prevent artificial price inflation.

questions.q: A "kick-out clause" (right of first refusal exception) in a sales contract allows the seller to:

opts.A: Reject any buyer who does not pay full price
opts.B: Require the buyer to use the seller's preferred lender
opts.C: Kick out a tenant currently occupying the property
opts.D: Continue marketing the property and require the buyer to remove their home sale contingency if a better offer arrives

questions.exp: A kick-out (bump) clause protects the seller when accepting an offer with a home sale contingency. It allows the seller to keep showing the property. If another acceptable offer comes in, the seller "bumps" the current buyer — who must either remove the contingency or terminate the contract.

questions.q: The settlement date (closing date) specified in the sales contract:

opts.A: Automatically extends if financing is delayed
opts.B: Is set by the lender without input from buyers or sellers
opts.C: Is a negotiated term that both parties agree to in the contract
opts.D: Must be at least 90 days from contract execution

questions.exp: The settlement date is a negotiated term in the contract. It can be extended by written agreement (amendment) of both parties, but it does not automatically extend — if financing delays occur without a written extension, the party causing the delay may be in breach unless "time is of the essence" provisions are waived.

questions.q: A buyer who receives the seller's counter-offer has which options available?

opts.A: Accept, counter-counter, or remain silent (which constitutes acceptance)
opts.B: Accept, reject, or issue another counter-offer
opts.C: Only accept or reject — no further counters are permitted
opts.D: Submit the counter-offer to the Real Estate Commission for approval

questions.exp: When the buyer receives a counter-offer, they may: (1) accept it as-is (contract formed), (2) reject it (process ends or buyer starts over), or (3) issue their own counter-offer (which then becomes the active offer for the seller to consider). There is no limit on the number of counter-offers.

questions.q: Radon disclosure requirements in Pennsylvania residential sales require sellers to:

opts.A: Disclose any known radon test results on the Seller's Disclosure Statement
opts.B: Mitigate any radon over 2 pCi/L before selling
opts.C: Perform radon testing before listing the property
opts.D: Provide a radon warranty to the buyer

questions.exp: Pennsylvania's Seller Disclosure Law requires sellers to disclose known material conditions, including radon test results they are aware of. Sellers are not required to test or mitigate — but known results must be disclosed. Buyers typically conduct their own radon testing as part of the inspection contingency.

questions.q: A real estate sales contract that does not close due to the seller's default entitles the buyer to:

opts.A: Only the return of their earnest money
opts.B: No remedy — market risk applies
opts.C: Return of earnest money PLUS the right to sue for damages or seek specific performance
opts.D: A penalty equal to 5% of the purchase price

questions.exp: When the seller defaults without legal justification, the buyer may: (1) get their earnest money back, (2) sue the seller for compensatory damages (additional costs, lost bargain), and/or (3) seek specific performance (court order compelling the sale). These remedies may be pursued individually or in combination.

questions.q: A buyer who removes all contingencies in writing and then fails to close is:

opts.A: In default, potentially forfeiting earnest money
opts.B: Protected by the inspection contingency
opts.C: Entitled to a full refund of earnest money
opts.D: Entitled to a 30-day extension automatically

questions.exp: Once all contingencies are removed in writing, the contract is firm. If the buyer then refuses to close without a legally excused reason, they are in default. The seller's remedy typically includes retaining the earnest money (if the contract provides liquidated damages) and/or suing for additional damages.

questions.q: A "walk-through" (pre-settlement inspection) is typically conducted to:

opts.A: Confirm the property's condition is as agreed (agreed repairs complete, seller's belongings removed)
opts.B: Renegotiate the price based on current market conditions
opts.C: Perform a complete home inspection before closing
opts.D: Satisfy the lender's appraisal requirements

questions.exp: The pre-settlement walk-through — typically 24–48 hours before closing — allows the buyer to confirm that agreed-upon repairs have been made, the seller has removed their personal property, and the property is in substantially the same condition as when the offer was made. It is not a substitute for a professional home inspection.

questions.q: When a property is sold "subject to" an existing mortgage, the buyer:

opts.A: Assumes full personal liability for the existing mortgage
opts.B: Takes title with the mortgage as an encumbrance but is not personally liable for the debt
opts.C: Pays off the existing mortgage at closing
opts.D: Must qualify for the existing loan with the lender

questions.exp: In a "subject to" purchase, the buyer takes title subject to the existing mortgage lien but does NOT assume personal liability. If the buyer stops making payments, the lender can foreclose, but cannot sue the buyer personally. The seller remains personally liable on the original promissory note.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST defines "merger" in real estate contract law?

opts.A: Two brokerage companies combining into one
opts.B: Two parcels being combined into one legal description
opts.C: A joint tenancy converting to tenancy in common
opts.D: The sales contract is merged into (superseded by) the deed at closing

questions.exp: The doctrine of merger provides that the sales contract merges into (is superseded by) the deed upon closing. This means most contract provisions are extinguished at closing — the deed becomes the operative document. Only provisions intended to survive closing (such as warranty covenants or indemnification clauses) remain enforceable after closing.

questions.q: The Loan Estimate (LE) is a disclosure that lenders must provide within how many business days of a mortgage application?

opts.A: 1 business day
opts.B: 2 business days
opts.C: 3 business days
opts.D: 5 business days

questions.exp: Under the TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rules, lenders must provide a Loan Estimate (LE) within three business days of receiving a completed loan application. The LE summarizes loan terms, projected monthly payments, and estimated closing costs so borrowers can compare loan offers.

questions.q: The Closing Disclosure (CD) must be provided to the borrower at least how many business days before closing?

opts.A: 1 business day
opts.B: 2 business days
opts.C: 7 business days
opts.D: 3 business days

questions.exp: Under TRID, the Closing Disclosure must be delivered to the borrower at least three business days before the scheduled consummation (closing). This gives the borrower time to review actual closing costs and compare them to the Loan Estimate before signing.

questions.q: A "conforming" conventional loan is one that:

opts.A: Meets Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac underwriting guidelines, including loan limits
opts.B: Has a fixed interest rate throughout its term
opts.C: Conforms to FHA insurance requirements
opts.D: Is insured by a private mortgage insurance company

questions.exp: A conforming loan meets the Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loan limits (which are adjusted annually), credit score, LTV, and debt-to-income ratio guidelines. Conforming loans can be sold in the secondary mortgage market. Loans exceeding the limit are "jumbo" (non-conforming) loans.

questions.q: USDA (Rural Development) loans are primarily designed for:

opts.A: Urban buyers seeking multi-family investment properties
opts.B: Eligible buyers purchasing properties in rural and some suburban areas with low-to-moderate incomes
opts.C: Commercial agricultural property purchases
opts.D: Any buyer regardless of location or income

questions.exp: USDA Rural Development loans offer 100% financing (no down payment) to eligible buyers with low-to-moderate incomes purchasing in USDA-designated rural and some suburban areas. Like VA loans, they require no down payment — but income limits and geographic requirements apply.

questions.q: The debt-to-income (DTI) ratio used by lenders measures:

opts.A: The ratio of the property's debt to its market value
opts.B: The borrower's monthly debt payments compared to gross monthly income
opts.C: The borrower's credit card balance to credit limit
opts.D: The down payment amount compared to purchase price

questions.exp: DTI = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income. Lenders use DTI to assess a borrower's ability to manage monthly payments. Most conventional lenders prefer a DTI of 43% or less (back-end ratio, which includes housing + all debts). FHA allows higher DTIs in some circumstances.

questions.q: Which type of loan is characterized by regular principal and interest payments that remain equal throughout the loan term?

opts.A: Balloon mortgage
opts.B: Adjustable-rate mortgage
opts.C: Interest-only mortgage
opts.D: Fixed-rate, fully amortized mortgage

questions.exp: A fixed-rate, fully amortized mortgage has equal monthly payments (same dollar amount) throughout the loan term. The payment mix changes — more principal and less interest over time — but the total payment stays constant, and the balance reaches zero by the last payment.

questions.q: An interest-only loan requires the borrower to:

opts.A: Pay only principal each month, deferring interest
opts.B: Make equal principal and interest payments
opts.C: Pay only the interest accruing each period, with the full principal due at the end
opts.D: Make quarterly interest payments and annual principal payments

questions.exp: During the interest-only period, the borrower's monthly payment covers only the interest. No principal is reduced. At the end of the interest-only period (or term), the full principal balance remains due — either as a balloon payment or transitioning to amortizing payments.

questions.q: The primary advantage of an ARM to the borrower at origination is typically:

opts.A: A lower initial interest rate than a comparable fixed-rate loan
opts.B: No prepayment penalty
opts.C: No risk of payment increases
opts.D: Guaranteed payment caps for the life of the loan

questions.exp: ARMs typically offer a lower initial ("teaser") rate compared to fixed-rate loans, making them attractive for borrowers who expect to sell or refinance before the rate adjusts, or who anticipate rising income. The trade-off is the risk of rate increases over time.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes a "short sale"?

opts.A: A sale that closes in less than 30 days
opts.B: A sale of a property with a short-term lease in place
opts.C: A sale where the net proceeds are less than the outstanding mortgage balance, with the lender's approval
opts.D: A foreclosure auction sale

questions.exp: A short sale occurs when a lender agrees to accept less than the full mortgage balance as payoff, allowing the property to be sold at market value (which may be below the loan balance). Short sales require lender approval and are an alternative to foreclosure for financially distressed sellers.

questions.q: In a deed of trust (used in some states), the three parties are:

opts.A: Lender, borrower, and appraiser
opts.B: Trustor (borrower), trustee, and beneficiary (lender)
opts.C: Grantor, grantee, and trustor
opts.D: Mortgagor, mortgagee, and guarantor

questions.exp: In a deed of trust (used in some states instead of a mortgage): the borrower (trustor) conveys title to a neutral third party (trustee) to hold as security for the lender (beneficiary). Upon default, the trustee can conduct a non-judicial foreclosure (trustee's sale) without court action.

questions.q: Mortgage points paid at closing to reduce the interest rate are also known as:

opts.A: Origination credits
opts.B: Escrow deposits
opts.C: Prepayment premiums
opts.D: Discount points

questions.exp: Discount points are prepaid interest paid at closing to buy down (reduce) the interest rate on the loan. Each discount point = 1% of the loan amount. Paying points makes sense if the borrower plans to keep the loan long enough to recoup the upfront cost through the lower monthly payments.

questions.q: A subordination agreement in real estate means:

opts.A: A lien holder with senior priority agrees to allow a new lien to take senior position
opts.B: A junior lien agrees to remain junior
opts.C: A senior lien agrees to become junior in priority
opts.D: Two lien holders agree to share equal priority

questions.exp: A subordination agreement changes lien priority by having the senior lienholder agree to move to a junior position, allowing a new (often refinanced) lien to take priority. For example, a first mortgage is subordinated so a construction loan can have first priority during construction.

questions.q: Which of the following mortgage types offers fixed monthly payments that gradually increase, with the early payments less than full interest (and the unpaid interest added to the principal)?

opts.A: Standard ARM
opts.B: Balloon mortgage
opts.C: Reverse annuity mortgage
opts.D: Negative amortization (graduated payment) mortgage

questions.exp: Negative amortization occurs when scheduled monthly payments are less than the interest accruing, causing unpaid interest to be added to the principal balance — making the loan grow rather than shrink. Some graduated payment mortgages and certain ARMs with payment caps can result in negative amortization.

questions.q: A Home Equity Line of Credit (HELOC) is BEST described as:

opts.A: A lump-sum loan secured by the home's full value
opts.B: An unsecured line of credit based on home value
opts.C: A revolving line of credit secured by the homeowner's equity
opts.D: A government-insured loan for renovation projects

questions.exp: A HELOC is a revolving line of credit (like a credit card) secured by the homeowner's equity. The homeowner may draw from it, repay, and redraw during the draw period. Typically secured by a second mortgage lien on the property, interest rates are usually variable.

questions.q: Mortgage fraud is a federal crime. Which of the following is an example of mortgage fraud?

opts.A: A buyer negotiating a lower purchase price
opts.B: Inflating the purchase price on the contract while secretly paying cash back to the buyer ("cash-back scheme")
opts.C: A seller offering concessions toward closing costs
opts.D: A buyer using gift funds for a down payment with proper disclosure

questions.exp: A cash-back scheme (fraudulent property flipping) involves misrepresenting the purchase price on official documents — overstating it to the lender while secretly returning cash to the buyer. This inflates the lender's loan basis and results in a loan greater than the property's actual value. It is a federal crime.

questions.q: Under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act (HMDA), lenders must:

opts.A: Offer loans to all applicants who apply
opts.B: Cap mortgage interest rates at the prime rate
opts.C: Collect and publicly report data on mortgage applications and originations, including demographic information
opts.D: Approve all FHA applications submitted

questions.exp: HMDA requires covered lenders to collect, maintain, and publicly disclose information about mortgage applications and originations — including geographic, race, gender, and income data. This transparency allows regulators and the public to identify potential discrimination patterns such as redlining.

questions.q: A reverse mortgage is designed for:

opts.A: Homeowners aged 62 or older who want to convert home equity into income without monthly payments
opts.B: Investors who want to flip properties
opts.C: Buyers who cannot qualify for a traditional loan
opts.D: Sellers who want to finance the buyer directly

questions.exp: A Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM or reverse mortgage) allows homeowners 62+ to borrow against their home equity — receiving cash, a line of credit, or monthly income — without making monthly payments. The loan balance grows over time and is repaid when the homeowner sells, moves out, or dies.

questions.q: The Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) requires lenders to:

opts.A: Approve all loan applications from protected class members
opts.B: Offer the same interest rate to all borrowers
opts.C: Require co-signers on all mortgage applications
opts.D: Notify applicants of the credit decision within 30 days and provide reasons if credit is denied

questions.exp: ECOA (Regulation B) requires lenders to notify applicants of their credit decision within 30 days of receiving a completed application. If credit is denied, the applicant is entitled to know the specific reasons. This allows applicants to understand denials and potentially correct errors or seek other lenders.

questions.q: The "front-end" (housing) DTI ratio includes:

opts.A: Principal, interest, taxes, insurance (PITI), and HOA fees, divided by gross monthly income
opts.B: All monthly debt obligations including student loans and car payments
opts.C: Only the monthly principal and interest payment
opts.D: Gross income minus all non-housing expenses

questions.exp: The front-end (housing) DTI ratio = PITI (principal + interest + taxes + insurance) + HOA fees ÷ gross monthly income. Most conventional lenders target a front-end DTI of 28% or less. The back-end DTI adds all other monthly debts and is typically capped at 36-43%.

questions.q: A "lock-in" (rate lock) in mortgage lending means:

opts.A: The lender has committed to approve the loan
opts.B: The lender guarantees a specified interest rate for a set period while the loan is processed
opts.C: The borrower cannot refinance for a set period
opts.D: The interest rate is tied to a market index for the life of the loan

questions.exp: A rate lock is the lender's commitment to hold a specific interest rate (and sometimes points) for a defined period — typically 30-60 days — while the loan is processed and closing is arranged. If market rates rise during this period, the borrower's rate is protected.

questions.q: The purpose of a real estate appraisal is to provide:

opts.A: The property's listing price
opts.B: An independent, supportable estimate of market value
opts.C: A guarantee of the property's future value
opts.D: The assessed value for tax purposes

questions.exp: An appraisal is an independent, impartial, and objective estimate of a defined type of value (typically market value) performed by a licensed or certified appraiser. It is not a guarantee of value, a listing price recommendation, or a tax assessment.

questions.q: Market value assumes a transaction with all of the following EXCEPT:

opts.A: Buyer and seller are typically motivated
opts.B: Both parties are well-informed
opts.C: Adequate time is allowed for marketing
opts.D: The seller is under pressure to sell immediately

questions.exp: Market value assumes a hypothetical transaction between an informed, willing — but not compelled — buyer and a similarly situated seller, with adequate time on the market. A seller under financial duress (forced sale) would likely accept below-market value — which does not reflect market value.

questions.q: The Sales Comparison Approach to value is MOST reliable for:

opts.A: Special-purpose properties (churches, schools)
opts.B: Income-producing commercial properties
opts.C: Properties with unique features that make comparison impossible
opts.D: Single-family residential properties with recent comparable sales

questions.exp: The Sales Comparison Approach is most reliable when there are numerous recent sales of similar (comparable) properties in the same market area — making it the standard approach for residential appraisals. It is less reliable for unique or special-purpose properties with few or no comparables.

questions.q: In the Sales Comparison Approach, when a comparable property has a feature the subject property lacks, the appraiser:

opts.A: Adds to the comparable's sale price
opts.B: Subtracts from the comparable's sale price (adjusts the comparable downward)
opts.C: Ignores the feature if it's small
opts.D: Adds to the subject property's estimated value

questions.exp: Adjustments in the Sales Comparison Approach are made to the comparable — not to the subject. If the comparable is superior (has something the subject lacks), subtract from the comparable's price. If the comparable is inferior, add to it. The adjustment makes the comparable equivalent to the subject.

questions.q: The Income Approach to value is MOST appropriate for:

opts.A: Income-producing properties (apartments, office buildings, retail)
opts.B: Vacant land with no income potential
opts.C: Owner-occupied single-family homes
opts.D: Special-purpose properties like hospitals

questions.exp: The Income Approach converts anticipated future income into a present-value estimate of the property's worth. It is most appropriate for properties purchased for their income potential — apartment buildings, shopping centers, office complexes. Buyers of investment properties typically purchase based on income expectations.

questions.q: Gross Rent Multiplier (GRM) is calculated as:

opts.A: Net Operating Income ÷ Sale Price
opts.B: Sale Price ÷ Net Operating Income
opts.C: Sale Price ÷ Gross Annual (or Monthly) Rent
opts.D: Gross Rent ÷ Operating Expenses

questions.exp: GRM = Sale Price ÷ Gross Annual (or Monthly) Rent. It is a quick valuation tool: GRM × Subject's Gross Rent = Estimated Value. Unlike the capitalization rate, GRM does not account for expenses, making it less precise but simpler to calculate.

questions.q: Net Operating Income (NOI) is calculated as:

opts.A: Gross Potential Income − Vacancy Allowance
opts.B: Effective Gross Income − Mortgage Payments
opts.C: Gross Income − Income Taxes
opts.D: Effective Gross Income − Operating Expenses (excluding debt service)

questions.exp: NOI = Effective Gross Income (Gross Potential Income − Vacancy & Collection Loss + Other Income) − Operating Expenses (not including debt service or income taxes). NOI is the income figure used in the income approach and to calculate the cap rate.

questions.q: The Cost Approach to value is MOST useful for:

opts.A: Income properties with predictable rental income
opts.B: Special-purpose or unique properties (schools, hospitals, churches) with few comparables
opts.C: Residential properties with many comparable sales
opts.D: Vacant land purchases

questions.exp: The Cost Approach (Land Value + Depreciated Improvement Value) is most reliable for unique or special-purpose properties where comparables are scarce (churches, schools, government buildings). It is also used for new construction, insurance purposes, and feasibility studies.

questions.q: Functional obsolescence in real estate is a loss in value caused by:

opts.A: Outdated design features or inadequate floor plan
opts.B: External market forces outside the property
opts.C: Physical deterioration from age and wear
opts.D: A flood that damaged the building

questions.exp: Functional obsolescence arises from design deficiencies within the property — such as an outmoded floor plan, outdated electrical capacity, lack of adequate bathrooms, or features that once added value but are now liabilities (e.g., a coal bin). It is caused by the property's design, not by external forces.

questions.q: External (economic) obsolescence is caused by:

opts.A: Roof deterioration from rain and weather
opts.B: An outmoded kitchen design
opts.C: Factors outside the property, such as a nearby industrial plant or neighborhood decline
opts.D: Poor maintenance by the property owner

questions.exp: External (economic) obsolescence comes from forces OUTSIDE the property boundaries — a nearby industrial plant, a declining neighbourhood, a new highway. It is the one form of depreciation the owner cannot cure, because the cause is not on the lot. Physical deterioration (wear, weather) and functional obsolescence (an outdated layout) both originate within the property.

questions.q: Which form of depreciation is generally considered "incurable" by the appraiser?

opts.A: Deferred maintenance (physical deterioration)
opts.B: Outdated kitchen appliances (functional)
opts.C: External obsolescence from a nearby highway
opts.D: A broken window (physical deterioration)

questions.exp: External obsolescence is almost always incurable because the property owner cannot eliminate the external negative factor (the highway, declining neighborhood, etc.). Physical deterioration and functional obsolescence may be curable (if the cost to fix is justified by the value increase) or incurable.

questions.q: In the Cost Approach, which method of estimating depreciation is MOST commonly used by appraisers?

opts.A: The income capitalization method
opts.B: The market extraction method only
opts.C: The age-life (straight-line) method
opts.D: The replacement cost new method

questions.exp: The age-life (straight-line depreciation) method calculates depreciation as: Effective Age ÷ Total Economic Life × Replacement Cost New. It is the most commonly used method in residential appraisal because of its simplicity. More detailed approaches (breakdown method) are used for complex properties.

questions.q: The principle of substitution states that a buyer will NOT pay more for a property than:

opts.A: The property's replacement cost
opts.B: The assessor's appraised value
opts.C: The cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute property
opts.D: What the seller originally paid plus improvements

questions.exp: The principle of substitution is the foundation of all three appraisal approaches: a rational buyer will not pay more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable alternative. This principle justifies comparing sales, estimating replacement costs, and analyzing income as substitutes for the subject property.

questions.q: The principle of contribution measures:

opts.A: How much each square foot of a home is worth
opts.B: The total value all improvements add to the land
opts.C: The market's overall demand for a specific property type
opts.D: How much a particular component adds to the total value of the property

questions.exp: The principle of contribution states that the value of any component of a property is measured by its contribution to the whole, not by its cost. A $50,000 swimming pool may add only $20,000 to market value if buyers in that market don't place high value on pools.

questions.q: Regression and progression principles state that:

opts.A: A superior property is pulled down by surrounding inferior properties (regression), while an inferior property benefits from superior surroundings (progression)
opts.B: Properties with declining values should be avoided
opts.C: All properties in a neighborhood should be priced equally
opts.D: Value always increases in proportion to improvement cost

questions.exp: Regression: a higher-value property surrounded by lower-value properties tends to lose value to the level of its neighbors. Progression: a lower-value property surrounded by higher-value properties tends to gain value. These principles explain why the "best house on the block" can be a poor investment.

questions.q: Reconciliation in the appraisal process means:

opts.A: Averaging the three approach values mathematically
opts.B: Submitting the appraisal to the lender for review
opts.C: Adjusting the value to match the contract price
opts.D: Weighing the evidence from each approach to arrive at a final value opinion

questions.exp: Reconciliation (final value correlation) involves the appraiser analyzing the results from the applicable approaches (sales comparison, income, cost) and, based on the purpose of the appraisal and the type of property, weighing their relative reliability to arrive at a single, defensible final value opinion.

questions.q: An appraiser who adjusts their value conclusion to match the purchase price (rather than reaching an independent conclusion) is committing:

opts.A: Dual agency
opts.B: Appraisal fraud (hit-the-number appraisal)
opts.C: Blockbusting
opts.D: A legitimate market-based adjustment

questions.exp: "Hitting the number" — inflating or adjusting an appraisal to match the contract price or loan amount rather than reaching an independent conclusion — is appraisal fraud. It violates the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice (USPAP), federal lending laws, and potentially criminal statutes.

questions.q: USPAP (Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice) governs:

opts.A: The ethical and performance standards that certified and licensed appraisers must follow
opts.B: The Commission's licensing requirements for salespersons
opts.C: How real estate agents price homes
opts.D: The maximum fees that appraisers may charge

questions.exp: USPAP, developed and maintained by the Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation, sets the minimum ethical and professional standards for appraisal practice in the United States. Compliance is required for appraisers performing appraisals for federally related transactions.

questions.q: When appraising a property, an appraiser must consider the principle of highest and best use, which is the use that is:

opts.A: Legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive
opts.B: Already established on the property
opts.C: Preferred by the owner
opts.D: Most common in the surrounding neighborhood

questions.exp: Highest and best use (HBU) is the reasonably probable use of property that produces the highest value — and it must meet all four criteria simultaneously: (1) legally permissible (zoning, deed restrictions), (2) physically possible (size, shape, topography), (3) financially feasible (generates positive returns), and (4) maximally productive (among feasible uses, produces the highest value).

questions.q: An appraiser differentiates between "effective age" and "chronological age" because:

opts.A: Chronological age is always used for tax assessment purposes
opts.B: Effective age reflects the actual condition of the improvements, which may be more or less than the actual years since construction
opts.C: Effective age is determined by the owner's improvements
opts.D: Chronological age determines the property's remaining economic life

questions.exp: Chronological age is simply the number of years since the building was constructed. Effective age reflects the apparent age based on the property's condition and maintenance — a well-maintained 30-year-old home may have an effective age of 15, while a poorly maintained 10-year-old home may have an effective age of 25.

questions.q: At closing, the Closing Disclosure (CD) shows:

opts.A: Only the buyer's closing costs
opts.B: Only the lender's fees
opts.C: The actual final loan terms, closing costs, and cash required for both buyer and seller
opts.D: A preliminary estimate of costs that may change after closing

questions.exp: The Closing Disclosure (replacing the old HUD-1) itemizes all final settlement charges — including loan terms, monthly payments, closing costs, prepaid items, and the cash required at closing — for both buyer and seller. It must match (within tolerances) the Loan Estimate provided earlier.

questions.q: The Pennsylvania Realty Transfer Tax is:

opts.A: Paid only by the buyer
opts.B: Paid only by the seller
opts.C: Based on the assessed value, not the sale price
opts.D: A 2% tax on the sale price, typically split equally between buyer and seller (1% each) plus any local add-on

questions.exp: Pennsylvania imposes a state realty transfer tax of 1% of the sale price. Most counties and municipalities add a local transfer tax (often 1% more), for a combined 2% statewide. By custom, it is typically split equally between buyer and seller (1% each), though negotiation is possible.

questions.q: Proration at closing is used to:

opts.A: Calculate the broker's commission split
opts.B: Determine the deed transfer tax
opts.C: Fairly divide ongoing expenses (taxes, rents, utilities) between buyer and seller based on the closing date
opts.D: Adjust the purchase price for market changes since contract signing

questions.exp: Proration allocates ongoing property expenses between buyer and seller as of the closing date. Items like property taxes, HOA dues, prepaid rents, and mortgage interest are divided so each party pays their fair share for their period of ownership. Prorations appear as debits and credits on the Closing Disclosure.

questions.q: At closing, a "debit" to the buyer means:

opts.A: Money owed to the buyer by the seller
opts.B: A charge the buyer must pay
opts.C: A credit the lender provides
opts.D: A reduction in the seller's proceeds

questions.exp: On the closing statement, debits are charges — money owed. A debit to the buyer represents cash the buyer must bring to closing (e.g., purchase price, closing costs, prorated expenses). A credit to the buyer reduces the amount they owe (e.g., earnest money deposit, loan proceeds, seller concessions).

questions.q: Prepaid interest at closing covers:

opts.A: The interest that accrues from the closing date to the end of the closing month
opts.B: All interest that will accrue during the loan term
opts.C: The buyer's first full monthly mortgage payment
opts.D: Interest penalties for paying the loan off early

questions.exp: Prepaid interest (also called per diem interest) at closing covers the interest that accrues from the closing date through the end of that month. The first full monthly payment (covering the prior month's interest) is typically due on the first of the second month after closing — this is "payment-in-arrears" mortgage interest.

questions.q: If property taxes are paid in arrears and the seller has NOT yet paid the current year taxes at closing, the seller should receive:

opts.A: A credit from the buyer for the taxes already paid
opts.B: No adjustment — the buyer pays all taxes going forward
opts.C: A credit for the buyer's share of taxes
opts.D: A debit for the taxes accrued during the seller's ownership period

questions.exp: When taxes are paid in arrears (common in Pennsylvania), the seller owes taxes for their period of ownership but hasn't yet paid them. The seller receives a debit (charge) on the closing statement — the buyer receives a corresponding credit — so the buyer can pay the full tax bill when due.

questions.q: Title insurance premiums are typically paid:

opts.A: Annually, like other insurance premiums
opts.B: As a one-time premium at closing
opts.C: Monthly as part of the mortgage payment
opts.D: At the time the title search is ordered

questions.exp: Title insurance is unique among insurance types in that it requires only a single, one-time premium paid at closing. The owner's policy typically remains in force for as long as the insured or their heirs have an interest in the property — no renewal premiums are required.

questions.q: RESPA prohibits which of the following at settlement?

opts.A: A settlement agent paying an unearned fee to a real estate agent for referring business
opts.B: The seller's proceeds being wired to their bank
opts.C: The buyer's attorney attending the closing
opts.D: The lender charging an origination fee

questions.exp: RESPA Section 8 prohibits the payment or receipt of fees, kickbacks, or anything of value for the referral of settlement service business. An unearned referral fee paid by a title company or settlement agent to a real estate agent for sending clients is a RESPA violation. Legitimate fees for actual services are permitted.

questions.q: In Pennsylvania, who typically conducts the closing settlement?

opts.A: The title company or an attorney
opts.B: The county recorder of deeds
opts.C: The listing broker
opts.D: The state Real Estate Commission

questions.exp: In Pennsylvania, residential real estate closings are typically conducted by a title company (title agent) or by an attorney. The title company handles the Closing Disclosure, coordinates payoffs of existing liens, disburses funds, and records the new deed and mortgage.

questions.q: The seller's net proceeds at closing are calculated as:

opts.A: The purchase price minus all debits (mortgage payoff, commission, closing costs, prorations)
opts.B: The purchase price minus only the broker's commission
opts.C: The listing price minus the buyer's closing costs
opts.D: The assessed value minus outstanding taxes

questions.exp: The seller's net proceeds = Purchase Price − (Mortgage Payoff + Broker's Commission + Transfer Taxes + Seller-paid Closing Costs + Prorated Expenses + Other Seller Debits). The seller's closing statement shows these items as a ledger, with the net check (or wire) as the remainder.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a "credit" to the buyer at closing?

opts.A: Origination fee
opts.B: Owner's title insurance premium
opts.C: The earnest money (deposit) already paid
opts.D: Prepaid homeowner's insurance

questions.exp: The earnest money the buyer already deposited is a credit — it reduces the amount the buyer must bring to closing. Other buyer credits include the loan amount, seller concessions, and any prorations in the buyer's favor (e.g., prepaid rents from a tenant). Origination fees, title insurance, and prepaid insurance are debits (charges) to the buyer.

questions.q: A lender's escrow account (impound account) at closing is established to:

opts.A: Hold the buyer's earnest money until closing
opts.B: Collect the seller's closing costs
opts.C: Collect funds monthly for future property taxes and homeowner's insurance payments
opts.D: Pay the broker's commission at closing

questions.exp: An escrow (impound) account is a special account held by the lender. The borrower's monthly payment includes a portion for property taxes and insurance, which the lender holds in escrow and pays on the borrower's behalf when due. This protects the lender's collateral from tax sales and uninsured losses.

questions.q: In a closing where the seller has a prepaid homeowner's insurance policy that extends beyond closing, the seller receives:

opts.A: A debit for the full premium
opts.B: No adjustment — the buyer gets the benefit without any charge
opts.C: A deduction from the commission
opts.D: A credit for the unused portion of the premium

questions.exp: If the seller has paid for insurance that extends beyond the closing date, the buyer benefits from the coverage for the remaining period. The seller receives a credit (reimbursement) for the unused (prepaid) portion, and the buyer receives a corresponding debit on the Closing Disclosure.

questions.q: After closing, the first document to be recorded at the county recorder's office is typically the:

opts.A: Mortgage (deed of trust)
opts.B: Deed
opts.C: Closing Disclosure
opts.D: Satisfaction of prior mortgage

questions.exp: After closing, the settlement agent records the deed first, transferring title to the buyer, then records the new mortgage. Recording is done in this order to establish the buyer as the owner of record before the mortgage lien is attached — ensuring the lender has a valid first lien on the buyer's property.

questions.q: The right of rescission under TILA gives a borrower the right to cancel certain mortgage transactions within:

opts.A: 24 hours of signing
opts.B: 5 business days
opts.C: 30 days
opts.D: 3 business days

questions.exp: TILA's right of rescission allows borrowers to cancel certain non-purchase refinances or home equity loans within 3 business days of closing (or 3 days from receipt of the required disclosures, whichever is later). The right does NOT apply to purchase money mortgages (purchase transactions).

questions.q: A seller who remains in the property after the closing date without the buyer's consent is:

opts.A: A holdover or trespasser who may be required to pay rent and face eviction
opts.B: Protected by the lease provisions of the sales contract
opts.C: Considered a licensee by the new owner
opts.D: Entitled to 30 days' notice before being asked to leave

questions.exp: Once the deed is delivered and the sale closes, the buyer is the new owner. If the seller remains beyond the agreed possession date without a written agreement, they become a holdover occupant or trespasser. The buyer may charge daily rent as specified in the contract and can initiate eviction proceedings.

questions.q: A settlement statement adjustment for a rent security deposit held by the seller means:

opts.A: The buyer receives a debit for the deposit
opts.B: The buyer receives a credit and the seller a debit for the security deposit that must be transferred
opts.C: The seller keeps the deposit as part of their proceeds
opts.D: The security deposit is paid directly to the departing tenant

questions.exp: Security deposits belong to the tenant — not the landlord. At closing, the seller (who holds the deposit) transfers it to the buyer. On the closing statement, the buyer receives a credit (they'll hold the deposit going forward) and the seller receives a corresponding debit.

questions.q: Which of the following typically appears on the seller's side of the closing statement as a CREDIT?

opts.A: Real estate commission
opts.B: Purchase price
opts.C: Transfer tax
opts.D: Mortgage payoff

questions.exp: The purchase price is a credit to the seller — it is the total amount the buyer is paying, which the seller receives (before deductions). Commissions, transfer taxes, and mortgage payoffs are debits (charges) to the seller, reducing their net proceeds.

questions.q: The annual percentage rate (APR) disclosed on the Closing Disclosure will typically be:

opts.A: Lower than the note interest rate
opts.B: The same as the note interest rate
opts.C: Higher than the note interest rate because it includes fees and other loan costs
opts.D: Set by the government and the same for all loans

questions.exp: The APR is always higher than the note (interest) rate because it includes the interest rate PLUS other financing costs (origination fees, points, mortgage insurance, etc.) spread over the loan term. APR is the true cost of borrowing and must be disclosed under TILA to allow loan comparison.

questions.q: In a 1031 exchange (like-kind exchange), a real estate investor can:

opts.A: Sell a rental property and pay no taxes ever on the gain
opts.B: Exchange any type of property (real or personal) for any other
opts.C: Exchange their primary residence for an investment property tax-free
opts.D: Defer capital gains taxes by reinvesting the proceeds in a like-kind investment property

questions.exp: A 1031 (like-kind) exchange under the Internal Revenue Code allows an investor to defer capital gains taxes on the sale of investment or business real property by reinvesting the proceeds in another like-kind property within strict time limits (45 days to identify, 180 days to close). The gain is deferred — not permanently excluded.

questions.q: A lease is BEST defined as:

opts.A: A deed that transfers ownership temporarily
opts.B: A verbal agreement to share property
opts.C: A license to use a portion of the landlord's property
opts.D: A contract granting a tenant the right to possess real property in exchange for rent

questions.exp: A lease is a contract between a landlord (lessor) and a tenant (lessee) that grants the tenant the exclusive right to possess and use real property for a specified period in exchange for consideration (rent). It creates a leasehold estate — the tenant has a possessory right, not ownership.

questions.q: An estate for years (fixed-term tenancy) ends:

opts.A: When either party gives 30 days' notice
opts.B: When the landlord decides to terminate
opts.C: Automatically at the lease expiration date, without notice
opts.D: Only when the tenant vacates the premises

questions.exp: An estate for years has a specific beginning and ending date. It terminates automatically when the term expires — no advance notice is required from either party. This is the standard residential or commercial lease for a fixed period (1 year, 2 years, etc.).

questions.q: A month-to-month tenancy (periodic tenancy) may be terminated by either party by giving:

opts.A: Typically one month's notice (one full rental period)
opts.B: One week's notice
opts.C: No notice — it terminates automatically each month
opts.D: Two months' notice in all cases

questions.exp: A periodic tenancy automatically renews for successive periods (month to month, week to week, etc.) until one party gives proper notice to terminate. The notice period equals one full rental period — typically one month's notice for a month-to-month tenancy. Pennsylvania may require different notice periods for residential tenancies.

questions.q: A tenant who stays beyond the lease term without the landlord's permission is:

opts.A: A tenant at will
opts.B: A periodic tenant
opts.C: A tenant at sufferance (holdover tenant)
opts.D: A licensee

questions.exp: A tenant at sufferance (holdover tenant) has no legal right to remain — they are staying beyond the lease term without the landlord's permission. The landlord may elect to evict them (as a trespasser) or accept rent, which may convert the holdover into a periodic (month-to-month) tenancy.

questions.q: In a gross lease, the tenant pays:

opts.A: Base rent plus all property operating expenses
opts.B: A fixed rent, with the landlord paying operating expenses
opts.C: A percentage of their business revenue plus base rent
opts.D: Only utilities, while the landlord pays everything else

questions.exp: In a gross lease, the tenant pays a fixed (flat) rent and the landlord is responsible for most or all operating expenses — taxes, insurance, maintenance, and utilities. This is the most common arrangement for residential rentals and some office leases.

questions.q: In a net lease (single net), the tenant pays base rent plus:

opts.A: Their share of building insurance only
opts.B: All taxes, insurance, and maintenance (everything)
opts.C: A percentage of gross sales
opts.D: Their share of property taxes

questions.exp: Net lease types build on each other. In a single net lease (N), the tenant pays base rent plus their share of property taxes. In a double net lease (NN), taxes AND insurance. In a triple net lease (NNN), taxes, insurance, AND maintenance/common area expenses — the most common for commercial retail properties.

questions.q: A percentage lease is MOST commonly used for:

opts.A: Residential apartments
opts.B: Government offices
opts.C: Retail tenants in shopping centers
opts.D: Industrial warehouse tenants

questions.exp: A percentage lease requires the tenant to pay a base rent plus a percentage of gross sales above a "breakpoint." It is primarily used for retail tenants in malls and shopping centers — the landlord's income rises with the tenant's business success, aligning incentives.

questions.q: Which lease type allows the rent to adjust periodically based on an economic index (such as the CPI)?

opts.A: Gross lease
opts.B: Net lease
opts.C: Index lease
opts.D: Ground lease

questions.exp: An index lease (also called an escalator lease) ties rent adjustments to changes in an economic index — most commonly the Consumer Price Index (CPI). As the index rises, rents increase automatically, protecting the landlord from inflation without requiring lease renegotiation.

questions.q: A ground lease is a long-term lease under which the:

opts.A: Tenant rents a fully improved building from the landlord
opts.B: Landlord retains all improvements at the end of the lease
opts.C: Landlord receives only a percentage of the tenant's income
opts.D: Tenant leases the land only and constructs improvements at their own expense

questions.exp: A ground lease is a long-term lease (often 50-99 years) of land only. The tenant builds their own improvements on the land. At lease end, ownership of the improvements typically reverts to the landowner. Ground leases are common in downtown commercial areas and airports.

questions.q: A covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease guarantees the tenant:

opts.A: That neighbors must not make excessive noise
